Ibn 'Ashur holds that "those who have lost themselves" are the polytheists, while others include the People of the Book. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain the loss as the loss of faith, while al-Tabari reports the view that it is the loss of one's dwellings and spouses in Paradise. Several commentators cite traditions on the merit of conveying the Quran and on the meaning of "whoever it reaches." Ibn 'Uthaymin draws from the verse a warning against lying about God in interpreting His verses and in declaring what is lawful or unlawful.

This verse describes what God will say to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection, after gathering them all together: He will rebuke them and ask where their associates are, the beings they claimed would intercede for them. The question is one of reproach rather than a genuine request for an answer. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that the associates are the idols and false gods, that they are called the polytheists' associates because the polytheists themselves gave them that status, and that the verb translated as claim means a false assertion; Ibn Abbas held that every instance of this word in the Quran means a lie. Opinions differ on how the opening phrase connects to the preceding verse. Al-Tabari links the day to what is said of the wrongdoers, who do not prosper in this world or on that day, while others treat it as a fresh statement. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that leaving the time-clause unspecified is meant to frighten. The word fitna in the next verse has been explained in several ways: their answer, their excuse, their argument or their speech, as reported by Qatada, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir. The passage thus warns against associating others with God and shows that the hope placed in idols' intercession will be exposed as baseless on that day.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection, when God gathers the polytheists together with the deities they worshipped and asks them where the partners they claimed would intercede for them now are. The commentators agree that their answer was only a denial of associating partners with God, sworn by God's name. They differ, however, on the meaning of the word fitna here. Qatada and, in one report, Ibn Abbas understood it as their excuse, while al-Samani and Muqatil took it to mean their speech or answer. Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understood it as their attachment to the idols, which ended only in disowning them when the hour of trial came. Abu Ubayda read it as the trial that left them without a proof.

The scholars also differ on how to read their oath, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take it as a plain lie, whereas al-Jubba'i, al-Qadi and al-Razi understand it as what they believed about themselves, and Ibn Juzayy sees it as a denial of what they knew. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur report that their haste to deny came from hoping to escape, like people overwhelmed by bewilderment. Finally, the differences in recitation, such as the verb forms "takun" or "yakun" and the case of "rabbana", hardly change the meaning.

God tells His Prophet to observe what will happen to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection. When they are asked where the partners they claimed are, those partners are nowhere to be found, and they swear by God that they were never polytheists. In doing so they lie against themselves, and what they had fabricated, namely the idols' intercession and benefit, vanishes from them. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that the lie here is the denial of association in the Hereafter, and that the vanishing means the idols bring them no benefit. Many explain the word fitna as meaning their argument, excuse or answer, that is, the denial and the oath they gave. The commentators differ on how people who see the truth could lie. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that people may lie on that Day out of bewilderment and confusion. Al-Qurtubi notes that most theologians say the Hereafter is a place of recompense in which there is no lying, so the statement means what they believed inwardly. This was the view of al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi, though al-Razi and al-Baydawi reject it as distorting the wording. Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur accept that the lie is real. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also relate from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the polytheists, seeing that only monotheists were forgiven, denied their association hoping to be saved, after which their mouths were sealed and their limbs testified against them. Some commentators also note differences in the recitation of the words takun and fitnatuhum, which do not change the general meaning.

This verse describes a group of polytheists who listen to the Prophet ﷺ recite the Quran without benefiting from it. The commentators explain that their hearts are covered by veils that prevent understanding, and their ears are heavy so they retain nothing; even when they see every sign they do not believe, and when they come to dispute with the Prophet they call the Quran merely the fables of the ancients. Most exegetes agree that the pronoun refers to the pagans of Mecca and that the images of veils and deafness express their hearts' remoteness from truth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read this figuratively, and Ibn Kathir considers that the figurative sense is the more apparent. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that their words aimed to deny the Quran's miraculous character. Ibn Kathir, al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin hold that God's making is real and a punishment for them, whereas the Mu'tazilites such as al-Jubba'i offer other readings, such as sleep imposed on night listeners or a mark on the hearts of those known to die in disbelief. Accounts name the listeners as Quraysh leaders such as Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who recounted Persian tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar. Opinions differ on who 'turn away from it': some say they forbid others from following the Prophet, others say they forbid the Quran itself, and Ibn 'Abbas links the verse to Abu Talib. All agree the verse rebukes those who listen without seeking guidance.

This verse describes the pagans who oppose the Prophet ﷺ and reject his signs: they forbid people from listening to the Qur'an and following the Prophet, and they keep themselves far from him as well. In doing so they destroy only themselves, without realising it. The commentators agree that the subject is the Quraysh unbelievers mentioned just before. The pronoun 'him' may refer to the Qur'an, as Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd hold, or to the Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn Abbas, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak hold. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the sense that they block people from following the Prophet while distancing themselves from him; al-Tabari prefers this reading because the surrounding verses speak of the polytheists as a whole rather than one individual. A different tradition, transmitted by Habib ibn Abi Thabit and Ata' ibn Dinar, links the verse to Abu Talib, who protected the Prophet without believing in him; al-Razi, however, finds the first reading closer to the context. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report both readings and the narratives attached to them. Most take 'destruction' to mean the ruin of the soul and the punishment to come, and the denial that they perceive it shows the depth of their blindness. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that placing the forbidding before the turning away shows how strongly they resent the message.

This verse describes the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they are brought to the Fire and stand before it, wishing they could be returned to the world so as not to deny the signs of their Lord and to be among the believers. The commentators differ on the sense of being placed before the Fire. Al-Tabari holds that "over" means "in", that is, they have entered it; al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and others mention that they were made to see it closely, were halted above it on the bridge, or came to know its reality; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya record these meanings without deciding among them. The answer to "if" is omitted to heighten the terror, so the reader imagines a dreadful scene. On the grammar of "nukadhdhiba" and "nakūna", opinions diverge. Most readers, with al-Tabari favouring them, take both in the nominative, attaching them to "we would be returned" or treating them as a statement. Ibn Amir reads the second as subjunctive, while Hamza and Hafs read both in the subjunctive as an answer to the wish. Sibawayh and Abu 'Amr take these words as an assertion rather than a wish, which makes God's words "indeed they are liars" fit better, since a wish cannot be called a lie; al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy reply that a wish carrying a promise can be described so. On "nay, there has appeared to them what they used to hide", al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir understand it as their hidden deeds or disbelief being exposed; Ibn al-Qayyim understands it as their inner acknowledgement of the truth of the messengers, which they concealed in the world. All agree that if they were returned they would revert to what they had been forbidden, and that their wish was driven by fear of punishment rather than sincere faith.

This verse describes the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they are made to stand before the Fire and wish they could be returned to the world so that they would believe and no longer deny the signs of their Lord. God replies that things are not as they wish, because what they used to conceal has now become clear to them. The commentators broadly agree that this wish did not come from a sincere desire for faith but from fear of punishment, and that God states that if they were returned they would go back to what they were forbidden, and that they are liars in their promise. Regarding what they had been hiding, opinions differ. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as their evil deeds or their hidden disbelief, while al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it was their polytheism, which they had denied before God until their own limbs testified against them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention the view that the verse concerns the hypocrites, while al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj hold that it refers to what the leaders concealed from their followers about the resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari focuses on the shameful deeds recorded in their books, and Ibn al-Qayyim argues that they knew the messengers were truthful and kept this knowledge hidden. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim also note that the wish arose from terror of the punishment rather than from a love of faith. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn Ashur stress the insincerity of the pledge, while Ibn Uthaymin draws from the verse that God's knowledge extends even to what is impossible. Commentators such as al-Alusi and al-Qasimi note several grammatical and recitation variants without deciding definitively between them.

This part of the verse quotes the words of the disbelievers who deny resurrection: there is only this worldly life of ours, and we will not be raised again. The commentators agree that the verse describes the denial of resurrection and the Last Day, the belief of those who expect no reward and fear no punishment after this life, and therefore do not care about the sins they commit, as al-Tabari explains. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that these words were spoken during the worldly life, so the verse depicts their stance before they witnessed the Hereafter. Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Qurtubi, links the phrase to the hypothetical answer 'had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden', so that these same words would be their speech if they returned. Al-Zamakhshari suggests attaching it to 'and they are surely liars', meaning they are liars in everything, and that this statement is itself proof of their lying. Ibn Atiyya notes that this first reading is the view of the majority. Ibn Kathir explains that their wish to return was motivated by fear of punishment rather than a genuine desire for faith, and he supports this with other Qur'anic verses. Al-Razi understands what they had concealed as the matter of resurrection itself. The commentators do not decide between these views and present them side by side.

The verse describes those who denied the Resurrection being made to stand before their Lord on the Day of Judgment. They are asked, "Is this not the truth?" They answer yes, swearing by their Lord, and are told: "Taste then the punishment for your disbelief." The commentators agree that "being made to stand" is a figure for being held for questioning and rebuke, like a guilty servant brought before his master. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the question as a rebuke, and say that "bala" affirms what was denied. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud also offer the sense of recognising God's decree or knowing Him fully. Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that what is shown to them is the punishment itself, while Ibn Abbas, quoted by Ibn Kathir, says the answer belongs to one particular station of the Resurrection, with other stations involving denial. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see the passage not as a new proof of resurrection but as a warning and rebuke. Al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur explain that "taste" is a metaphor for experiencing. All agree that disbelief is the cause of the punishment, though they differ on its object: the resurrection or the punishment itself.

The commentators explain that the verse means those who denied meeting God, that is the resurrection and the reckoning, have lost their bargain, having exchanged faith for disbelief and obedience for disobedience. When the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they cry out in regret over what they neglected, carrying their burdens on their backs. Most agree that loss means the forfeiture of good and the arrival of punishment, that hasra is intense regret, and that wizr means sin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others note that the pronoun in 'fīhā' may refer to the worldly life, the Hour, the transaction or the good deeds; al-Tabari prefers the transaction, while Ibn Kathir leaves the possibilities open. On how the burdens are carried, al-Tabari, al-Suddi, Amr ibn Qays and Ibn Kathir hold that it is literal: the deed appears in a foul form and the disbeliever is made to ride it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it as a picture of hardship and suffering, and Ibn Juzayy allows either reading. Ibn Atiyya and al-Zajjaj take 'sa'a' to function like 'bi'sa', meaning evil is what they carry. Al-Razi adds that the loss is the forfeit of capital and profit for one who did not prepare for the afterlife.

This verse says that the life of this world is, in its reality, only play and diversion with no lasting benefit, while the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God, and that a sensible person should understand this. The commentators agree that it answers the disbelievers who said, "There is only our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected." Al-Tabari explains play as what passes quickly and leaves regret behind, like a child's game. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi give three views: worldly life is brief like a toy; its pursuits are play when they do not serve the Hereafter; or its people are like players busy with trifles, a view attributed to al-Hasan. Al-Razi stresses that worldly life is not blameworthy in itself, since happiness in the Hereafter is earned in it. He reports that Ibn 'Abbas applied the verse to the life of the unbeliever alone, while he and al-Qurtubi take it to cover every fleeting pleasure, and he offers long arguments for the baseness of bodily pleasures. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it as a call not to cling to what perishes, and read "for those who are mindful of God" as implying that whatever is not the work of the pious is play. Ibn 'Ashur sees in it both an encouragement to believers and a discouragement to polytheists. On the readings, Ibn 'Amir's "wa-la dar al-akhira" is explained as an idafa of a kind found in "mosque of the congregation", or as an ellipsis; the common reading is preferred by al-Razi and al-Qurtubi. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur distinguish play, which seeks pleasure, from diversion, which distracts from what matters.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that He knows what grieves him in what the polytheists say, and reassures him that, in truth, they do not deny him in conviction, since they knew him as truthful and trustworthy, even calling him al-Amin; it is the wrongdoers among them who deny God's signs while knowing them. The commentators offer two opposed readings. The first holds that they do not deny him in private, knowing his truthfulness, but deny him openly out of enmity; Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir among others hold this. The second holds that they do not deny his person but what he brings; al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take this line, and al-Tirmidhi reports from Abu Jahl the words: we do not call you a liar, but we call what you brought a lie. Al-Tabari judges that both readings, with the shadda and without it, are sound and each has an acceptable meaning. The first form means to accuse someone of lying, while the second means to find him to be a liar or to prove him so. Several report that the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq and Abu Jahl, when Abu Jahl admitted the Prophet's truthfulness yet refused to follow him for fear of losing preeminence. The verse then consoles the Prophet: messengers before him were called liars, they were patient, and God gave them victory, for none can change the words of God.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet ﷺ: messengers before him were denied and harmed, yet they endured patiently until God's help reached them, and no one can alter the words of God, that is, His promise of victory. The accounts of the messengers steady the heart. The commentators agree that the verse is a consolation and an exhortation to patience, following the example of earlier prophets, and that the phrase 'none can change the words of God' confirms the promise of help. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij read it as consolation for the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by Abu Hayyan, holds that 'they do not call you a liar' is not an absolute denial of denial but a figure of speech like a master telling a servant that they did not insult him but insulted me, a view al-Nasafi reports and al-Qasimi discusses critically. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi discuss the grammar of 'ma' and of the coordinated verb 'udhu', while Abu Hayyan weighs several analyses of the subject of 'jaaka'. Ibn 'Abbas takes God's words to be His promises; al-Zajjaj extends them to His commands and decrees, and al-Razi draws from this a point about divine decree. Ibn 'Ashur notes that patience under denial and harm is a constant pattern for the messengers. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that the Prophet, sent to all mankind, must bear greater trials. Readings are also noted: Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read 'yukadhdhibunaka' without gemination, and Ibn 'Amir reads 'udhu' without the waw.

This verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ over his deep grief at his people's refusal. God tells him that if their turning away weighs heavily upon him, and if he were able to dig a tunnel into the earth or climb a ladder to the sky to bring them a sign, he should do so; the sense, however, is that he cannot, and the answer to the condition is left understood. Commentators explain that the nafaq is a passage underground and the sullam a ladder or means of ascent, some citing a line of poetry. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, see the verse as showing the Prophet's intense eagerness for his people to believe, and hold that the demanded sign lies beyond his power. On God's words that He could have gathered them upon guidance, al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir read it as meaning that God would have guided them all had He willed, but in His prior knowledge He did not will it, an argument Sunni scholars use against the Qadariyya. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya take it that He could have compelled them by a coercive sign, which He does not do since it would go against wisdom. Al-Razi develops a reasoned argument about divine power and will. Finally, the warning not to be among the ignorant is generally read as a prohibition against grief and anguish over what cannot happen, some holding that it addresses the community rather than the Prophet himself, and Ibn Uthaymin clarifies that such a prohibition does not imply the Prophet committed the fault.

This verse states that only those who truly listen and accept the truth respond to the Prophet's call, while the disbelievers are likened to the dead, who neither hear nor respond. The commentators differ on who is meant by the dead. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Tha'alibi understand them to be the disbelievers, whom God will raise in their disbelief on the Day of Resurrection and gather, so that they hear only under compulsion, the verse thus being a warning to them. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di also mention the view that the dead are literal dead, used as an example to show that they do not respond until they are raised. Ibn Uthaymin considers that both meanings may be held together, containing both a threat to the disbelievers and a reply to those who deny resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that God is able to revive the hearts of these people with faith, which the Prophet cannot do. Al-Razi notes that ignorance is a death of the soul. Several scholars distinguish between istijaba and ijaba: the first means acceptance, while the second may be a refusal. They agree that the hearing meant is that of acceptance and understanding rather than mere hearing. The verse ends by affirming that all will return to God to be judged.

This verse reports the demand of obstinate opponents of the Prophet: why has no sign (an extraordinary proof) been sent down to him from his Lord? God tells the Prophet to answer that God is able to send down a sign, but that most of them do not know the wisdom behind withholding it. The commentators agree that the demand was made out of stubbornness, since many signs had already come to them, and that God's power is complete. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy explain that God knows that a forced sign followed by refusal to believe would bring immediate punishment, as happened to earlier peoples; al-Tabari also stresses their ignorance of divine wisdom. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi say the sign meant is one that compels faith, such as the mountain lifted over the Children of Israel. Al-Razi lists several readings of their demand and holds that the Quran is itself a sufficient sign; Ibn Ashur sees the demand as a way of rejecting the proof the Quran provides. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri stress that guidance and misguidance belong to God's will. The next verse, about creatures that form communities like humans, is explained by Mujahid as distinct species known by their names, and by Ibn Qayyim as a call to reflect on divine wisdom.

This verse states that every creature that crawls on the earth and every bird that flies on its wings is a community like yours, created by God, whose sustenance and term are determined, and that the Book has omitted nothing. Ibn 'Abbas and others explain "communities like you" as distinct kinds, each known by its name, Qatada sees the birds, humans and jinn as communities, and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna finds in humans a resemblance to each animal in its character. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari stress the resemblance in creation, provision and divine care. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet for al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, while al-Razi takes it to be the Quran. On the gathering at the end, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean the death of animals, whereas Abu Hurayra and most commentators take it to mean resurrection on the Day of Judgment, supported by the hadith of the hornless sheep avenged against the horned one, which some read as a picture of perfect justice. The scholars thus differ on details, but all agree that God's care extends to every creature.

This verse describes those who denied God's signs, meaning the Qur'an and the proofs brought by the Prophet, as deaf and dumb to the truth and wandering in the darkness of disbelief, ignorance and stubbornness. Al-Tabari explains that the disbeliever does not look at God's signs to take a lesson from them, and forgets that his Creator did not make him in vain. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others compare their condition to that of a deaf-mute lost in darkness who cannot find the way. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi conclude that these attributes mean their senses no longer serve to guide them. As for the phrase 'whom God wills to lead astray, He leads astray, and whom He wills, He places on a straight path', Sunni commentators such as al-Baydawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take it literally, holding that guidance and misguidance rest on God's will. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Jubba'i understand misguidance as abandonment and the withholding of grace (lutf), guidance being that grace. Ibn 'Ashur explains divine misguidance as the consequence of a person's obstinacy and affirms that God does not command indecency. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that God's will is joined with wisdom and with the servant's own actions. Al-Qurtubi sees in the verse proof that God willed the disbeliever's straying so as to carry out His justice, while those who seek guidance receive God's grace.

God instructs His Prophet to ask the polytheists: tell me, if God's punishment comes upon you, or the Hour overtakes you, will you call upon anyone other than God to remove it, if you are truthful in claiming that your idols benefit and harm? Most commentators read the question as a rhetorical one that binds them to their own experience: in genuine distress, a person calls only upon God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the punishment as death or the ruin that struck earlier nations, while al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi also include the calamities of this life, and Ibn 'Ashur reads the verb "come upon" as a metaphor for befalling. The majority hold that the Hour is the Day of Resurrection, though some take it as the moment of death. The exegetes agree that "Nay, it is Him you call upon" negates the calling of idols and restricts it to God, that the removal of harm is subject to God's will, and that "what you associate" is forgotten either in the sense of being distracted or of being abandoned, with al-Razi and al-Baydawi accepting both. Grammarians debate the phrase "arayaytakum" at length: the Basrans take the kaf as a mere particle of address with no grammatical role, the Kufans treat it as an object, and most read it as meaning "tell me", with the interrogative clause serving as the second object. The recitations differ: Nafi' softens the hamza, al-Kisa'i drops it, and the others pronounce it fully. Ibn Kathir, as-Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin see in the verse a proof of monotheism and an appeal to human nature, while Sayyid Qutb reads it as a portrait of the innate disposition, the fitra.

This verse describes how, when God's punishment or the Hour comes upon them, the polytheists call on God alone and beg Him for deliverance. God may remove what they ask Him to remove if He wills, while they forget the idols and partners they associated with Him. The commentators agree that the verse is an argument against the polytheists based on what they admit in times of distress. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi stress that the granting of their request is subject to God's will, and al-Razi and Ibn Ashur conclude that the answer is not automatic but depends on divine wisdom. On the meaning of "forget", Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn take it as heedlessness caused by terror, whereas al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take it as abandoning and rejecting the idols, and al-Hasan describes it as turning away like one who has forgotten.

On the grammar, the Basrans regard the kaf in "arra'aytakum" as a mere particle of address with no grammatical role, while al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' treat it as an object; al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the phrase here means "inform me". The conditional answer is left implied, and the scholars differ on how to reconstruct it. Most identify the Hour with the Day of Resurrection, while some take "God's punishment" to mean worldly calamities, or even death and its signs.

Al-Razi and al-Jalalayn stress that people turn to God in adversity. Ibn Kathir, al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Uthaymin conclude that God answers the distressed even if they are disbelievers, and that He answers the wronged.

This verse states that God sent messengers to many nations before Muhammad ﷺ, and when they rejected them, He tested them with hardship and affliction: poverty and want on one side, and sickness and loss of life or property on the other. The commentators explain that the purpose was that they would humble themselves before God and turn back from disbelief. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand this as humility, submission, repentance and sincere devotion, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as admitting one's sin and believing, and al-Razi explains that supplication means submitting and giving up rebellion. Most agree that al-Ba'sa' means poverty and hunger and al-Darra' means sickness and the loss of lives and property, though al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba and others give closely related definitions, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the two words can stand in for each other. On the question of why they did not humble themselves when Our punishment came, al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that they had no excuse except obstinacy, hardened hearts and Satan making their deeds seem fine. As for their forgetting what they had been reminded of, most take it to mean they ignored the warning, so God opened the doors of worldly good to them as a gradual test, a reading supported by Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi through the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir. Ibn 'Ashur suggests that God delayed total destruction after first striking them with lesser troubles. The scholars close with praise of God for the destruction of the wrongdoers, which al-Zamakhshari counts among the greatest of blessings and Ibn Kathir links to the ruin of the disbelievers.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls how God sent messengers to earlier peoples and tested them with hardship and affliction, meaning poverty, hunger and loss of property, and sickness and bodily harm, so that they would humble themselves and repent. They did not. Here "falawla" means "why then did they not", so the sense is a denial of humility at the moment the punishment came. Most commentators, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that the reason for this refusal was the hardness of their hearts, that is their stubborn persistence in disbelief, with Satan making their deeds seem good so that they took pride in them. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say that the word "la'alla" expresses a hope as a human observer would conceive it, not a real expectation on God's part; al-Razi refuses to ascribe to God a hope in the literal sense and explains the passage through the way God deals with people. Many understand humility to mean faith, repentance and submission, and the negation also covers someone whose prayer is not sincere. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi see in the verse a rebuke for failing to call upon God. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di connect it to what follows, where God gradually leads the unbelievers toward ruin by granting them blessings and then seizes them suddenly; Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir on this. All explain "mublisun" as despairing, stricken or bewildered, and al-Tabari notes that it describes one who falls silent when his argument fails. Several observe that trial by adversity and by prosperity alike serves to educate and test. Finally, al-Zamakhshari understands the closing praise as a call to thank God for the destruction of wrongdoers.

This verse speaks of peoples to whom God sent messengers and who rejected them. God tested them with hardship and illness so that they would humble themselves before Him, but they did not, their hearts hardened and Satan made their deeds seem fair to them. Then, because they forgot the warning they had received and did not learn from the trial, God opened for them the doors of every good thing. When they rejoiced in these gifts with the joy of arrogance, He seized them suddenly, and they were left in despair. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand this opening as istidraj, a deceptive respite and a divine stratagem, and Ibn Kathir supports this reading with the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir. As for forgetting, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj take it to mean abandoning and turning away rather than mere lapse of memory, while al-Zamakhshari compares the alternation of hardship and ease to a caring father dealing with his child. On the meaning of mublisun the commentators differ: Ibn 'Abbas says those who despair, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' say those who are grieved and silenced when their argument fails, Mujahid says those who are disgraced, and al-Suddi says those who are destroyed. They agree, however, that the final praise is for the destruction of the wrongdoers, meaning the polytheists. Ibn 'Ashur sees a warning to the Quraysh, who may suffer the same fate. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the blamed joy is the joy of arrogance, not the joy of gratitude for God's grace.

This verse states that the people who did wrong were wiped out to the last one. The word dabir is explained by most as the last of the people, the one who follows behind; al-Tabari, al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the root, so that they were uprooted, while al-Wahidi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir stress that not one of them remained. Lexicographers differ: Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba read it as the last, al-Asma'i as the origin, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya combine both in the sense of following and succession.

Commentators link this verse to what precedes it. The peoples had first been struck with hardship and illness so that they would humble themselves, but they did not repent. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that Allah then opened to them every door of good, a test and a respite, and they cite the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir on istidraj, which Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also report while noting its weak chain. Ibn 'Ashur reads these favours as a sign that fear of God had not been awakened, whereas al-Qasimi stresses the element of requital.

On the closing praise, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it as a reminder that thanks to God are due for the destruction of wrongdoers, al-Razi offers several reasons for it, and Ibn 'Ashur reads it as praise for the cleansing of the earth. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that wrongdoing is the cause of the punishment.

God commands His Messenger to ask the polytheists: if God takes away your hearing and sight and seals your hearts, what god other than Him could bring them back to you? This is an argument against worshipping other than God, since no one but Him holds power to harm or benefit. The commentators agree that the meaning is the removal of the senses and reason, that the verb 'took' means removed, and that the 'signs' are the proofs God varies in many ways, rational arguments, encouragement and warning, and lessons from earlier peoples. The verb 'yasdifun' means turning away. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada render it as turning aside, Ibn Abbas as swerving, and al-Suddi as hindering others from the truth. They differ over what the pronoun 'bihi' refers to: al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' take it to mean the act, that is, 'with what was taken'; others take it to refer to hearing, with sight and heart included; others take it to mean the guidance implied by the context. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note variant readings, particularly those of Nafi' and Hamza. Al-Razi, al-Biqa'i and Abu al-Su'ud explain that hearing is mentioned first because it is the channel of revelation, and that 'thumma' expresses astonishment at turning away after the signs have been made clear. Ibn Kathir adds that this deprivation may also mean being unable to use these faculties legitimately. A following verse threatens divine punishment, and al-Hasan takes 'suddenly' to mean at night and 'openly' to mean by day, while Mujahid understands it as sudden surprise versus visible approach.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to ask the idolaters: tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you suddenly, without warning, or openly, after signs have preceded it, will anyone perish except the wrongdoers? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and others understand wrongdoing here as polytheism, worshipping others than God and abandoning His worship. Ibn al-Jawzi adds that the destruction includes the polytheists and those like them. The commentators agree that 'baghta' means a sudden arrival with no prior sign, and 'jahra' means a punishment preceded by signs that announce it. Mujahid explains that the sudden arrival happens while they are secure, and the open one while they are watching.

The scholars differ on the time of day. Al-Hasan, as reported by al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, takes the sudden one to mean at night and the open one by day. Al-Razi and al-Alusi find this reading inconsistent with the preceding context. Many read the interrogative form as a negation or rebuke: only the wrongdoers perish. Al-Razi notes that real destruction falls on the wrongdoers, since the righteous gain great rewards even through hardship. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a promise that the believers will be saved, and explains that 'the wrongdoing people' refers to the associators.

On the linguistic side, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi observe that 'baghta' carries an idea of concealment, which explains its contrast with 'jahra'. Variant readings are noted, such as vowelled forms of both words and the verb read in the active voice. These points remain secondary to the general sense of the warning.

This verse states that the messengers were not sent to produce miracles according to the demands of the people, but to bring good news to those who obey, namely reward and Paradise, and to warn those who disobey of punishment and the Fire, as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir explain. Whoever believes and does righteous deeds will have no fear about what lies ahead and no grief over what they left behind, whereas those who denied God's signs will be struck by punishment because of their transgression, that is, their departure from obedience. The commentators broadly agree on this general meaning but differ on details. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir restrict the fear and grief to the Hereafter, while Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shawkani discuss the grammar of the word man and the role of the fa'. Al-Razi notes that massa means contact without separation. As for fisq, Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean disbelief, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean lying. Al-Baghawi explains that righteous action means doing good, whereas al-Alusi and Ibn 'Uthaymin connect it to sincerity and following the Prophet's example. Al-Jalalayn limits fear and grief to the Hereafter.

This verse states that the messengers were sent only to bring good news and to warn, not to produce the miracles that people demanded. Those who believe and act righteously have nothing to fear or grieve over, while those who denied God's signs will be touched by punishment because of their deviance. Al-Tabari explains that those who denied were those who rejected the proofs the messengers brought, and that punishment befalls them as a consequence. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the verb "touch" to mean that the punishment reaches the wrongdoers, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain the image by describing punishment as if it were a living agent that strikes them. As for fisq, most commentators render it as disbelief and departure from obedience; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Ashur report that Ibn Zayd took every occurrence of the word in the Quran to mean lying, while Ibn 'Ashur gives it the general sense of going beyond the bounds of good. Al-Razi observes that the punishment is linked to the deviance, and disputes al-Qadi's argument that every deviant would share the same fate, without settling the matter. Al-Alusi notes that some readers understood the connection between the wrong and the punishment as causal. Modern commentators such as Ibn 'Uthaymin draw lessons about the need for messengers and divine justice. They agree on the general meaning of the verse and do not debate legal questions arising from it.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the polytheists the limits of his mission: he does not possess the treasures of God, meaning His provision and power, he does not know the unseen except what is revealed to him, and he does not claim to be an angel, but only follows what is revealed to him. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi, agree that the verse answers the pagans' demands for extraordinary signs, and that it affirms the Prophet's humanity and servanthood. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, followed by most, take the blind man to be the disbeliever and the seeing man the believer, while Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr understand them as the astray and the rightly guided, and others as the ignorant and the knowing. As for the unseen, many distinguish between absolute knowledge, which belongs to God alone, and relative knowledge that some people may have; Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the Prophet knows the unseen only through revelation. The question of whether angels are superior to prophets has been debated: al-Jubba'i and al-Zamakhshari cite the verse in support of angelic superiority, whereas al-Qadi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi reply that the verse addresses the pagans' objections rather than that question. Likewise, some draw from it an argument against analogical reasoning, while Ibn 'Ashur, al-Qurtubi and others hold that this matter rests on other evidence.

God commands His Prophet to warn with the Quran those who fear being gathered before their Lord, since they will have no protector or intercessor apart from Him, so that they may become God-fearing. The commentators agree that the warning addresses those who accept the resurrection, not those who deny it, but they differ on who is meant. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir understand it mainly as believers who dread the Last Day, while al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi include anyone who affirms the resurrection, whether Muslim or People of the Book, and al-Hasan restricts it to believers. Al-Razi argues that even a doubter fears the gathering, since no rational person is certain it will not occur. Al-Zamakhshari treats the clause about having no protector as a necessary circumstantial phrase, a view Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss. Al-Tabari takes the verb "fear" to mean "know". On the denial of intercession, most explain that intercession happens only by God's permission, which does not contradict the intercession granted to believers. Regarding the occasion of revelation, several reports say that Quraysh leaders asked the Prophet to drive away poor believers such as Bilal, Ammar and Suhayb, and the following verses were revealed in response. Ibn Kathir considers some of these accounts doubtful, since the surah is Meccan.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ not to drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. He is not accountable for their reckoning, nor they for his, so driving them away would make him a wrongdoer. The commentators agree that the 'calling upon' here means worship and remembrance of God, but they differ on its form. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan and Qatada take it to be the prescribed prayers. Ibn Abbas, in one report, says the five daily prayers, while Qatada and Mujahid, in another, mean only the dawn and afternoon prayers. Al-Nakha'i takes it as the remembrance of God, al-Dahhak as worship in general, al-Tabari as learning and reciting the Quran, and al-Zajjaj as calling upon God in sincere monotheism. As for 'seeking His face', Ibn Abbas explains it as seeking God's reward, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat the face as a reference to the divine Essence. Most exegetes report that the verse was revealed about poor believers such as Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb and Khabbab, when notables of Quraysh asked that they be pushed away so they could sit with the Prophet. Some reports say he was inclined to agree, hoping for their conversion. Ibn Kathir considers some of these narrations weak, since the sura is Meccan. On the phrase 'you are not accountable for their reckoning', al-Hasan and most scholars take it as the reckoning of deeds; others take it as the reckoning of provision, and Ibn Bahr as sufficiency. Most say the pronoun refers to the believers, while others say it refers to the polytheists.

This verse explains that God tests people through one another: He makes some rich and others poor, some noble and others lowly, some strong and others weak. The leaders of Mecca mocked and rejected the believing poor, asking how God could have favoured them with guidance over themselves, and God replies that He knows best who is truly grateful. Al-Tabari, al-Samani, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the trial as the test of the powerful by their followers: a noble who sees a lowly person embrace Islam before him may refuse to submit out of pride. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan read the lam as a lam of consequence, and take the test to be God's abandonment that leads the unbelievers to such speech; they interpret it in line with the Mu'tazili rejection of God creating evil, while the Sunni scholars hold that God creates both good and evil. Al-Razi uses the verse in the debate on whether God creates human acts, and al-Jubba'i and al-Ka'bi offer other readings. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Nahhas note that the lam may be causal or one of consequence, and that the question may be sincere rather than denying. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari relate the occasion of revelation: the leaders asked the Prophet to send away the poor believers from his gathering, and the following verses command him to honour them. Ibn 'Ashur sees envy and pride behind this attitude, and holds that the verse points to the fact that spiritual merit does not depend on wealth.

This verse describes believers who came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking guidance. God instructs him to greet them first as an honour, and to tell them that their Lord has prescribed mercy upon Himself: whoever does evil out of ignorance, then repents and mends his conduct, will find God forgiving and merciful. The commentators agree on this plain meaning: a warm welcome for the believers and a promise of forgiveness upon repentance and reform. They differ on who is addressed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take them to be the poor believers whom the Prophet was told not to drive away, and Ikrima reports that the Prophet always greeted them first. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi also report that they were people who had committed grave sins and asked the Prophet for guidance. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy relate that the verse concerns Umar, who had advised turning these men away and afterwards apologised. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that it applies generally to every believer. On the meaning of 'ignorance', Mujahid understands it as not knowing the lawful from the unlawful, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as acting on a sin without weighing its consequences, and Ibn Kathir notes that some take it to mean any act of disobedience. On recitation, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read the word 'annahu' with a fatha as an appositive to mercy, while most readers use a kasra as an explanatory clause. All agree that repentance requires regret, giving up the sin, and making amends.

This verse says that just as God has set out His proofs against the idolaters throughout this sura, He clarifies His signs so that truth is separated from falsehood and the path of the wrongdoers becomes plain, so that it can be avoided. The commentators agree on the general sense of clarification. Al-Tabari explains that God sets out His argument on every truth that the people of falsehood deny, and Ibn Kathir adds that the aim is to distinguish the way of guidance from the way of error. Ibn Qutayba understands the word for detailing as bringing the verses one after another rather than all at once. Al-Tabari prefers the nominative reading of "the way", noting that Tamim treat it as masculine and the people of the Hijaz as feminine, and that both are well attested. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya take the address to be to the Prophet, while the intended audience is his community. Al-Razi argues that naming the way of the wrongdoers is enough to show the way of the believers, since truth and falsehood have no middle ground. Ibn Zayd identifies the wrongdoers as those who urged the Prophet to drive away the weak believers, whereas most commentators understand them more broadly as the disbelievers. The commentators do not settle these differences; their main point is that clarity protects people from going astray.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to tell the polytheists that he has been forbidden to worship the things they call upon besides God, and that he will not follow their desires in this matter; if he did, he would be astray and not among the rightly guided. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the meaning is that God has turned him away from polytheism and forbidden it to him, and that the 'desires' are what their souls urge them to, namely worshipping idols and driving away the weak from the Prophet's gathering, as al-Baghawi notes. The commentators agree that desire does not lead to guidance and that following it leads to error; al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari take the verse as a call to follow evidence rather than blind imitation. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan see the relative pronoun 'those whom' as following the unbelievers' view, who treated the idols as rational beings, while Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi take 'calling upon' to mean worshipping, and others understand it as naming them gods or calling on them in one's needs. There is a minor reading difference over 'dalaltu', pronounced with a fatha by most readers, which is the more common usage according to al-Tabari, and with a kasra in the dialect of Tamim. Most commentators connect the verse to what precedes it, namely that God details the signs so that the path of the wrongdoers becomes clear. The following verses, according to most, state that the Prophet has a clear proof from his Lord, that the punishment they seek to hasten is not in his power, that judgment belongs to God alone, and that had it been in his hands the matter would already have been settled, God knowing best who the wrongdoers are.

The verse tells the Prophet to say to the idolaters that he stands on a clear proof from his Lord, that they have denied it, and that the punishment they seek to hasten is not in his hands. Judgment belongs to God alone, who declares the truth and is the best of judges. The commentators agree that the clear proof means certainty about God's oneness and the revelation, and that the punishment they demand is the one they mocked for, such as calling for stones to fall from heaven. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take the pronoun to refer to the Lord, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan link it to the proof or to the Quran. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya distinguish the punishment from the miracles the Quraysh demanded, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers the first reading.

On the word yaqussu, the readers of Hijaz and Asim read it from qasas (to relate), while most readers read yaqdi (to judge). Al-Tabari and al-Razi prefer the reading from judging, which fits the phrase best of the judges. Abu Hayyan notes the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, yaqdi bil-haqq. As for the sense of judgment, some understand it as separating truth from falsehood through reward and punishment, while others take it as deciding to bring down or delay the punishment. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the Prophet did not have the power to hasten the punishment, and that had he had it, he would have used it against them.

The commentators also agree that the verse shows God alone controls when punishment comes, and that God knows best who the wrongdoers are.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the idolaters that if the punishment they are demanding were in his power, the matter would be settled between him and them at once by their destruction; but the decision rests with God alone, who knows best the wrongdoers and the time of their punishment. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the power to hasten or delay the punishment belongs to God. The wrongdoers are the associators who give worship to others than God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the punishment meant is the one the Quraysh challenged them with, while al-Mawardi, citing al-Zajjaj, allows that it may also refer to demands for miracles made out of their proper time. Ibn 'Abbas, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, says the Prophet would not have granted them a moment's respite and would have destroyed them; al-Zamakhshari adds that this would have been out of anger for his Lord, a phrasing Abu al-Su'ud finds unfitting for the dignity of the statement. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi reject the view attributed to Ibn Jurayj that 'the matter would be settled' means 'death would be slaughtered', since it borrows a meaning from a verse in Maryam. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the account of Ta'if, where the Prophet declined the offer of the angel of the mountains and preferred to wait in hope that God would bring from their descendants people who worship Him alone.

This verse states that the keys of the unseen belong to God alone, and that no one else knows them. He knows what is on land and at sea, and no leaf falls, no grain lies hidden in the darkness of the earth, and nothing fresh or dry exists without being recorded in a clear Book. The commentators agree that God's knowledge encompasses both universals and particulars. They differ on the meaning of 'keys of the unseen': al-Suddi and others take them as treasuries of the unseen, Ibn 'Abbas as the stores of decrees and provision, al-Dahhak and Muqatil as the treasures of the earth and knowledge of when punishment will descend, 'Ata' as what is hidden of reward and punishment, and others as the final terms of lives and the ends of deeds. A report from Ibn 'Umar, cited by al-Bukhari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, states that these keys are five, the ones mentioned at the end of Surat Luqman. On 'the sea', al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and most scholars take it literally, while Mujahid takes 'the land' to mean deserts and 'the sea' to mean inhabited places with water. As for the 'clear Book', al-Muqatil and al-Baghawi identify it with the Preserved Tablet, while al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari take it as God's perfect knowledge. Al-Qurtubi stresses that claiming knowledge of the unseen through divination or astrology is a grave sin. Interpretations of 'the fresh and the dry' vary between what grows and what does not, the living and the dead, or water and dry land.

This verse states that God takes souls at night through sleep, withdrawing the self by which one perceives and acts, just as He does at death. He also knows what you earn by your limbs during the day, then He rouses you in daytime so that the appointed term of your life is completed. Then to Him is your return, and He will inform you of what you did and repay you for it. The commentators agree that tawaffi here means sleep, jaraḥtum means earning or committing, ba'th means waking, and the appointed term is the span of life until death. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi take the pronoun in fihi to refer to the day, while Ibn Juraij holds that the awakening happens in a dream; Ibn Kathir considers the first view more apparent. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan mention that some restricted the address to the disbelievers as a warning, but most read it as general. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi see the verse as an argument against those who deny resurrection, since whoever can cause sleep and awakening can raise the dead. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi stress that sleep is not a real death, and al-Qurtubi holds that the true nature of this withdrawal is known only to God. Al-Nasafi relates that each sense has its own spirit withdrawn during sleep, while the spirit of life is taken only at the end of the term. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shawkani note that tawaffi basically means taking something in full. Al-Sha'rawi reflects on sleep as a sign of God's power.

In this verse God declares that He is the Subduer, supreme over His servants, to whom everything yields by His power and majesty, and that He sends over people guardians, angels who count and record their deeds. When death comes to one of them, God's messengers take his soul, and they never neglect what they are commanded. The commentators agree that the guardians are angels who record deeds and watch over the person, and that the purpose of this watch is to restrain the believer from sin, knowing that his deeds will be displayed on the Day of Resurrection. They differ on the meaning of 'above', which al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi take as superiority of power, rank and dominion rather than spatial direction. They also differ about the guardians. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Qatada identify them as the angels who succeed one another by night and by day, while others say they record permitted acts, sins and good deeds, and do not see the intentions of the heart. As for the messengers who take the soul, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan and Qatada hold that they are assistants of the Angel of Death, who seize the soul and then hand it over to him. Al-Kalbi says the Angel of Death hands it to angels of mercy or of punishment, while Muqatil holds that the plural refers to the Angel of Death alone, out of honour. All agree that they do not neglect what they are ordered to do. The next verse says that all will be returned to God, their true Master, who alone judges and is the swiftest of reckoners. Commentators differ on whether those returned are angels or humans, most holding humans. God knows best what He intends.

This verse states that after death, when the souls have been taken by the messengers sent by God, people are returned to God, their true master, to whom alone belongs the judgment, and who is the swiftest of reckoners. The commentators differ on who is returned. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Mawardi say the angels who took the souls are returned, or that the return means that the management of affairs goes back to God alone, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi understand it as the return of all people to God's judgment on the Day of Resurrection. As for the word mawla, al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani take it to mean master and owner rather than helper, which avoids a conflict with the verse saying that disbelievers have no mawla. Most explain al-haqq as the just God who judges only by truth, or as one of His names, and some read it in the accusative as praise. All agree that judgment belongs to Him alone on that day. On the speed of the reckoning, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi connect it to a report that He reckons all creation in the time it takes to milk a sheep, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it as a speed that needs no counting or deliberation. Al-Razi also links the verse to his account of how acts shape the soul, a view he presents as a philosophical reading of the text.

God tells His Prophet to ask the polytheists who rescues them from the darkness of land and sea, meaning the perils where one loses the way and fears destruction. They then call upon God humbly and in secret, vowing to be grateful if He saves them. The commentators agree that the "darknesses" are a metaphor for dangers and hardships, and that in distress a person turns to God alone. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir explain it through the traveller who loses his way and calls upon God, and they read in this sense the report about the Quraysh who travelled by land and sea. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that these darknesses may be literal, such as drowning or being swallowed by the earth, and al-Razi sees in the verse a revelation of the human nature that turns to God in distress and then forgets once saved. The works record varied readings of "yunajjikum" (doubled or not), "khufyatan" (with damma or kasra) and "anjana" (with ta or nun), which do not change the core meaning. The next verse states that God saves them from this and from every distress, yet they still associate partners with Him; al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya read this as a rebuke that highlights the gravity of their conduct. Commentators agree that the question serves as a reproach and a demand for acknowledgement, and that true gratitude includes faith and obedience, though they differ on the details. Some also connect these trials to punishments from above or below, or to strife among people, but opinions on these points remain varied.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to ask the idolaters who rescues them from the darkness of land and sea, meaning the perils they face when lost or overwhelmed. In such moments they call upon God humbly and sincerely and vow to be grateful if He delivers them. The answer the Prophet is to give is that God alone rescues them from this and from every distress, yet they then associate others with Him. The commentators agree that the darknesses are a figure for dangers and trials, that karb is a grief that seizes the soul, and that the question serves rebuke and reproach. They differ on the doubling of the verb and on the vowel of khufya, which they treat as two close dialects. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the punishment from above and below as stoning and engulfment, while Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read it as unjust rulers and wicked subordinates. Al-Razi notes that the perils of sea and desert include drowning and losing one's way, and he holds that attachment to other than God can be a hidden form of idolatry. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also cite hadiths in which the Prophet ﷺ asks that his community not be destroyed by a punishment from above or below, nor have its violence turned against itself, with variant accounts of the occasion of revelation. The commentators agree that the verse shows God's power both to deliver and to punish, and that people sincere in distress often forget after being saved.

God commands His Prophet to tell the polytheists that the One who rescues them from the darkness of land and sea and from every distress is alone able to send a punishment upon them from above, such as stones, a flood or a blast, or from beneath their feet, such as an earthquake or a sinking of the ground, or to confuse their affairs so that they split into rival factions and kill one another. Commentators explain that the punishment from above refers to stoning, the cry and the flood, and that from beneath the feet refers to being swallowed up by the earth and to earthquakes, an interpretation favoured by al-Tabari and most exegetes. Ibn Abbas, however, reports that 'from above' means unjust rulers and 'from beneath your feet' means wicked servants and the lowly. On the meaning of 'mixing you into factions', Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understand it as divergent desires and discord, while al-Zajjaj describes it as turmoil rather than agreement. The scholars differ over who is addressed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the verse as a warning to the disbelievers, while Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-'Aliya take it as a reference to this community, and al-Hasan divides the verse between the two groups. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi reconcile these views by holding that it includes both believers and unbelievers. Finally, 'see how We vary the signs' means that God presents the proofs in many ways so that they may understand.

The commentators explain that the pronoun in « wa-kadhdhaba bihi » refers most often to the Qur'an, which his people rejected though it is the established truth. Some, including Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir in one reading, take it to refer to the threatened punishment, whose coming is certain. Al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan hold that the address concerns the unbelievers mentioned earlier, while Ibn 'Atiyya accepts that the pronoun may return to the threat itself. As for « lastu 'alaykum bi-wakil », the meaning is: I am not a guardian over your deeds, nor one empowered to force you to believe; I am only a warner. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kathir. Al-Wahidi, al-Sam'ani, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that some hold the verse abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others, such as Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, see it as a statement without abrogation, or as valid in its outward sense. On « likulli naba' mustaqarr », al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that every report has a reality and an end at which truth is separated from falsehood, whether in this world or the next, as Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said. Al-Suddi links it to the battle of Badr, whereas al-Hasan connects it to the strife among the Companions or to punishment in the Hereafter for denying resurrection. Zajjaj reads it as a warning of what will befall them in this world. « wa-sawfa ta'lamun » is a pure threat, which may point to punishment in the Hereafter or to military defeat.

The commentators explain that this verse states that every announcement of punishment has a fixed time when it will occur, neither earlier nor later, and that the disbelievers will know its truth when it arrives. The word naba' means a weighty news item, and mustaqarr is the time when it settles and takes place. The verse follows the statement that your people denied it though it is the truth, and it addresses the Prophet, who is not their guardian and cannot compel them to believe.

Most exegetes read it as a threat. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that every report will have its reality, either in this world or in the Hereafter. Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi add that it will come at a set time and place without delay. Al-Suddi reports that what was promised was fulfilled at Badr, and al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi also note this. Al-Hasan limits it to punishment in the Hereafter because they deny resurrection, while al-Zajjaj takes it to refer to punishment in this world.

Scholars differ on the pronoun in "bihi". For al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir it refers to the Quran, for al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan to the punishment mentioned earlier, and for al-Tabari to the threat in general. As for "you are not a guardian over them", al-Hasan reads it as: I do not count your deeds to repay you, I am only a warner, while al-Zajjaj reads it as: I will not force you to believe. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some held the verse abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others said it is a statement that is not abrogated.

Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as an answer to the question of when the punishment will come.

This verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ, and according to many commentators the believers with him, to turn away from those who engage in vain talk about God's verses, mocking, denying and disparaging them, not to sit with them, and to rise until they move on to another subject. If Satan makes him forget and he sits with them, he should rise as soon as he remembers. The commentators agree that the 'plunging' refers to idle talk about the Quran. They differ on the addressees and the target. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi take the target to be the polytheists who deny the verses and mock them, while Ibn Juraij reports that the polytheists came to listen to the Prophet and then mocked him. Ibn 'Abbas extends it to anyone who strays in religion outside the Book and the Sunna, Ibn Kathir and Muhammad al-Baqir to anyone who distorts God's verses, and Ibn Sirin to followers of innovations. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that the address is to the Prophet but the rule concerns the community. On the phrase 'those who fear God bear no account for them', most read it as freeing the righteous from blame when they keep away. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a permission to sit with them when necessary, and some hold it abrogated by the verse in al-Nisa: 'you would then be like them'. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the reminder as a warning meant to make them guard against such conduct. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also discuss whether prophets can forget, a question on which scholars differ.

This verse says that believers who fear God bear no responsibility for the account of those who mock God's signs. Their duty is instead to admonish the mockers, in the hope that they will refrain. Most commentators link it to the occasion described in the previous verse, when Muslims asked how they could sit in the Sacred Mosque and circle the Kaaba if they had to stand up every time the idolaters mocked the Qur'an. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the permission to stay seated was given on condition of reminding and admonishing them.

The commentators agree that reminding means warning the mockers, either by words or by standing up and showing disapproval, and that being present is not sinful so long as one does not approve. They differ on what the reckoning refers to. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer several readings: the sins of the mockers, the punishment of their speech, or the difference between their account and that of the believers. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that the word for reminder can be read in the accusative as a verbal noun or in the nominative as a predicate.

On abrogation the scholars disagree. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Suddi and Mujahid hold that the permission was abrogated by Qur'an 4:140, which forbids sitting with mockers until they change the subject. Al-Qurtubi, citing al-Qushayri, and Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti hold that the verse is not abrogated, since it states a fact. Ibn Sa'di adds that if admonishing would only increase their evil, withdrawing is the required course. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir read the phrase so that they may refrain as a hope that they will hold back out of shame or dislike.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from those who have taken their religion as play and diversion, mocking God's signs and treating the faith they were charged with as a pastime, deceived by the life of this world. He tells him to warn, through the Qur'an, that a soul may be delivered to ruin for what it has earned: it will have no protector or intercessor apart from God, and no ransom, however great, will be accepted from it. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that the verb tubsala means to be handed over to ruin and held in pledge for one's deeds. Others, such as al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd, render it as being punished or seized, and Ibn 'Abbas as being disgraced. They explain that hamim is scalding water that the damned drink, adding to their torment for their disbelief.

The scholars differ on the verse's ruling. Qatada and Ibn Zayd, as al-Tabari reports, hold that it was abrogated by the verse of fighting, while Mujahid takes it as a warning with no abrogation, a view followed by Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy. Al-Razi understands the verse as describing people who use religion to reach worldly ends. Al-Farra' and al-Sam'ani report that every community has a festival, and that the Muslims' festival consists of prayer and glorification.

Lexicographers cited by al-Tabari and al-Mawardi explain that the root basl originally means prohibition, and Arabic verses are quoted in support. Al-'adl, according to most exegetes, means the ransom.

God instructs His Prophet to ask the polytheists, in reproach: shall we call upon, besides God, something that can neither benefit nor harm us, and turn back on our heels after God has guided us? The commentators liken the apostate to one whom the devils have lured into the wilderness, bewildered, while companions call him to the right path and he does not answer. All agree that true guidance is God's guidance, that is Islam, that everything else is error, and that we are commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds. They differ on who the calling companions are: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them to be believers calling to guidance, whereas al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and others also mention devils or unbelievers who lead astray. On the occasion of revelation, it is reported that it concerned Abd al-Rahman, son of Abu Bakr, who invited his father to idolatry, though the commentators do not settle the question, and A'isha rejected the report. On the verb istahwat, al-Razi takes the sense of falling, while others take that of being drawn by desire. Ibn Mas'ud's reading clarifies the sense of guidance. The lam in li-nuslima is read by grammarians as a purpose particle, as a superfluous particle, or as equivalent to the preposition ba. The following verses glorify the Lord through the creation of the heavens and earth, the resurrection, and His knowledge of the unseen and the seen.

This verse reports that some polytheists invited certain believers to worship their idols. God then instructs His Prophet to ask them, in disapproval, how they could call upon what neither benefits nor harms them, and turn back after being guided, like someone the devils have led astray in the land, bewildered, while his companions call him to the right path. It then states that true guidance is God's guidance, that one must submit to the Lord of the worlds, perform the prayer, be mindful of Him, and that to Him you will be gathered. According to Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir, the verse was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman, son of Abu Bakr, who invited his father to idolatry, a report others trace to Ibn 'Abbas. Commentators agree that the pronoun in 'and be mindful of Him' refers to the Lord of the worlds, and that the guidance meant is Islam. They differ on the grammar of 'and that you establish the prayer': al-Zajjaj, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi link it to 'that we may submit', al-Zamakhshari to the position of that phrase, and al-Tabari reads the particle as equivalent to 'that'. Al-Razi explains the shift to the presence form as distinguishing the disbeliever, treated as absent, from the believer, treated as present. Regarding the trumpet, most exegetes take it as a horn into which Israfil will blow, while a minority read it as a plural of 'form'.

This verse affirms that Allah alone created the heavens and the earth in truth, meaning with wisdom and not in vain, and that His word is true: when He wills a thing, He says to it "Be," and it is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain "in truth" as wisdom and justice, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it may also mean beneficence toward the servants or the true word. As for "the day He says, Be, and it is," al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi take it to mean the Day of Resurrection, al-Kalbi takes it as the command to the heavens to become trumpets, and al-Zajjaj offers several possibilities. The commentators agree that dominion belongs to Allah alone on the day the Trumpet is blown. The main disagreement concerns the word as-Sur. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi understand it as a horn into which Israfil blows, relying on the prophetic reports, whereas Abu 'Ubayda, Qatada and, in one narration, Ibn 'Abbas read it as the plural of "form," with souls breathed into the bodies. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya suggest that "Knower of the unseen and the seen" may describe the One who created, or be a separate subject. The verse closes by naming Allah the All-Wise, the All-Aware, which warns against associating partners with Him and affirms His power to resurrect.

This verse records Ibrahim's rebuke of his father Azar for taking idols as gods, and his declaration that he and his people are in clear error. Most commentators hold that Azar was the name of Ibrahim's father: Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir accept this, and Ibn Kathir adds that genealogists give the father the name Tarah, so that he had two names, as Jacob was also called Israel. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say that Azar was the name of an idol, so the sense becomes 'do you take Azar as a god?' or an ellipsis is assumed. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Sulayman al-Taymi read it as a term of blame meaning 'crooked' or 'mistaken', and al-Dahhak gives the Persian sense of 'old man'. Readers differ on the vowel: most read it with a fatha because it is a non-declinable foreign proper name, while Ya'qub reads it with a damma as a direct address. Ibn Ashur notes that the harshness of the address follows earlier gentle appeals recorded in Surat Maryam, and comes after the father persisted in disbelief. Al-Razi argues that Azar was Ibrahim's paternal uncle, relying on the purity of the Prophet's ancestry, but most exegetes reject this view. All agree on the central point: worshipping idols is an error no sound mind can miss, and Ibrahim stated it plainly without compromise.

This verse states that God showed Abraham, peace be upon him, the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that is, their sovereignty and signs, so that he might be among those who have certainty, after he had rebuked his father and people for worshipping idols. Commentators differ on the nature of this showing. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Mujahid take it as a sight: the heavens and earth were opened for him up to the Throne and what lies beneath, though Ibn Kathir notes that the narrations describing this are not authentic. Al-Tabari holds that he was shown the dominion of the heavens and earth, namely the sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees and seas. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi consider it a showing of insight and intellect, by which he grasped the realities of creation and their pointing to the Creator, which they regard as higher than mere sight. On the word malakut, al-Zajjaj and others take it as an intensive form of mulk, while Ikrima said it is a Nabataean word. Regarding certainty, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya define it as knowledge that arises after doubt is removed through reflection, and some connect it not only to monotheism but also to prophethood and the message. On grammar, some regard the waw as superfluous and the lam as attached to an implied verb, while others link the clause to an implied cause. Most agree that the verse describes Abraham's progression from reasoning to certainty, while differing on how this showing took place.

The commentators read this verse within the context of Abraham's debate with his people, who worshipped the stars, the sun, the moon and idols. When night covered him and he saw a star, which al-Tabari and others identify as Venus and others as Jupiter, he said "This is my Lord" as a supposition and a way of drawing his people into reflection.
