When the star set, he said he did not love things that set, since setting and moving are signs of createdness rather than divinity. The same reasoning is applied to the moon and then the sun, moving from the lesser to the greater. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that setting is a clearer argument than rising, because it is a movement accompanied by disappearance. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others regard the passage as a debate meant to refute the people. Al-Tabari also reports a view that this took place during Abraham's childhood before proof had been established; Ibn Kathir rejects it, holding that prophets are protected from such error. Several exegetes offer grammatical readings: an implied interrogative, an implied verb of saying, or the phrase "according to your claim". The commentators agree that setting proves createdness, that worship belongs to God alone, and that Abraham declared his disavowal of polytheism once the proof was established. Accounts of his birth in a cave and of Nimrod's dream are reported by some but are not required to understand the verse.

This verse describes how Abraham, seeing the moon rise, said to his people, speaking in their own terms, this is my lord. When it set, he said that unless his Lord guided him he would be among the misguided. The commentators agree that the passage belongs to Abraham's debate with his people, who worshipped the stars, the sun, the moon and idols, and that his aim was to refute that worship by reasoning. A heavenly body that sets is shown to move and vanish, and so cannot be a god. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi place the passage within the dispute with the idolaters, Abraham voicing their claim in order to overturn it afterwards. Al-Razi, who devotes a long discussion to it, notes that some scholars take the words as Abraham's private reflection, possibly before he reached puberty, while others place them after he had come of age. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the words cannot express settled belief and are best read as a question or a test. Al-Zamakhshari explains that setting is a stronger proof than rising, since it is a movement accompanied by concealment. Nearly all agree that guidance belongs to God alone, and that Abraham asks to be kept firm on the right path. Some narrations about his birth in a cave are mentioned, but many scholars reject them as not fitting the context of the debate.

This passage recounts how Abraham, seeing the sun rise, said, this is my lord, this is greater, and then, when it set, declared his innocence of what they associated with God. The commentators agree that Abraham did not believe the sun was lord, and that the purpose was to refute the worship of the heavenly bodies through argument. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the words were a debate with his people and a way of making the argument clear. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the proof rests on the setting rather than the rising, since setting is a movement accompanied by disappearance and is therefore more evident. Al-Razi gives several readings, including a quotation of the opponent's view, a rhetorical question, or a strategy to draw the listeners in. Ibn Kathir considers the debate reading the most correct and rejects the idea that it happened in childhood. Others, including al-Tabari in one reading, present it as a personal search for truth. On grammar, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain that the masculine demonstrative is linked to the sense of light or of the rising one, and avoids attributing feminine marks to the divine. All agree that the heavenly bodies are changing creatures and that the Creator of the heavens and the earth alone deserves worship.

The commentators explain that this verse relates Abraham's words once the truth had become clear to him: he declares his disavowal of his people and of association with God, and turns his intention and worship toward God alone, the Creator of the heavens and the earth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain 'turning my face' as sincerity in worship and devotion to God alone, while 'hanif' means one who turns away from polytheism toward monotheism and adheres to the upright religion. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the root meaning is inclination. Most exegetes conclude that Abraham was never a polytheist, which the verse states plainly. On the surrounding passage about the star, the moon and the sun, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators understand it as a debate with his people, in which the setting of the stars shows that they are created and not divine; Ibn Kathir adopts this reading and rejects the view that it was a private reflection in childhood, which other scholars defend. Al-Razi offers several senses for 'this is my Lord': a reproachful question, a stratagem to win the listener's attention, or a repetition of the opponents' own claim. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a way of leading them gradually to the truth. Al-Alusi and al-Baydawi note that the preposition 'li' expresses submission and service rather than direction in space.

This verse recounts how Abraham's people argued with him about the oneness of God. He replied: Will you dispute with me about God, when He has guided me? The commentators explain that Abraham does not fear the idols they associate with God, because they can neither harm nor benefit, and that any harm reaching him could only come by the will of God alone, whose knowledge encompasses all things. He then urges them to reflect.

The exegetes agree that the dispute concerned God's oneness and the rejection of partners, and that the people threatened Abraham with harm from their idols. Many read the exception "unless my Lord wills" as disconnected, meaning "but", so that the only true fear is of God's will. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as connected with an implied time, meaning except at the moment my Lord wills; Ibn 'Ashur notes that this in effect covers all times. Al-Razi offers several meanings of divine will, such as a sin that deserves punishment or a trial through hardships.

As for "Will you not then take heed?", most take it as a call to recognise that these deities are lifeless objects that neither harm nor benefit, and that only the Creator deserves worship. Ibn Kathir and others observe that Abraham's refusal to fear the idols is itself a proof of their powerlessness.

The commentators conclude that those who affirm God's oneness are the most secure, that security and guidance belong to those who have not mixed their faith with wrongdoing, and that this wrongdoing means associating partners with God, according to the hadith transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, although al-Zamakhshari understands it as the sin that makes a person a transgressor.

This verse records Abraham's argument against his people, who threatened him with their idols. He asks how he could fear idols that neither harm nor benefit, when they themselves do not fear God, who created and provided for them, and whom they associate with others without any authority revealed to them. He then asks which of the two groups deserves security: the one that worships the One who holds harm and benefit, or the one that worships what cannot harm or benefit. The commentators agree that the 'injustice' in the verse 'those who believed and did not mix their faith with injustice' means associating partners with God, as confirmed by the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in the two Sahihs citing Luqman's words. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn treat the verses as Abraham's argument. Scholars differ on its scope: Ali held that it concerns Abraham and his companions alone, Ikrima applied it to the emigrants, while others took it as general. On who speaks the answer, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq see it as God's own judgment separating the parties, Ibn Jurayj as the reply of Abraham's people, and al-Zajjaj as Abraham questioning and answering himself. Al-Zamakhshari reads the word 'labs' as mixing faith with a sin that makes one a wrongdoer, while al-Razi and Ibn Kathir hold that injustice here means shirk.

This verse states that complete security and right guidance belong to those who believed without mixing their faith with wrongdoing, and most commentators understand that wrongdoing here means associating partners with God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take it as the answer to Abraham's question to his people about which of the two groups deserves security more. They rely on the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, in which the Prophet explained that the meaning is Luqman's words, "Indeed, associating others with Allah is a tremendous wrong." Al-Tabari also cites companions such as Abu Bakr, Ali, Salman and Hudhayfa giving the same meaning.

The commentators differ on who is speaking. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that it is God's own judgment separating Abraham from his people, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that it is Abraham's own words. Others see it as the reply of Abraham's people, or as a general divine ruling, a view attributed to Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd. Ali, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya, restricts it to Abraham alone, and 'Ikrima restricts it to the emigrants to Medina.

The meaning of "wrongdoing" is also debated. Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites extend it to sins that make their doer a transgressor, concluding that a grave sinner has no security. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and others reply that the Prophet's explanation takes precedence. Ibn Sa'di offers a graded reading: whoever avoids both association and sins attains complete security and guidance, while whoever avoids only association attains their foundation.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to the argument Abraham presented to his idolatrous people, by which he refuted the worship of the stars, the sun, the moon and idols. He asked them which of the two groups deserved security more: those who worship one God without associating anything with Him, or those who worship many gods that can neither harm nor benefit, and they conceded the point themselves. God had given Abraham this argument, either by guiding him to it or by teaching it to him, and his standing was thereby raised above his people. The exegetes agree that raising the degrees means elevation in knowledge, wisdom and rank, and the verse closes by stating that your Lord is wise in His dealings and knowing of who deserves such elevation. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir hold that the wrongdoing mentioned in the phrase 'have not mixed their belief with wrongdoing' is polytheism, relying on the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud and Luqman's words to his son. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it more broadly as any form of disobedience, and they leave the question open between them. As for what 'this argument' refers to, some point to the statement of the believers mentioned by Mujahid, others to Abraham's whole speech, and al-Razi and Ibn Kathir to all his arguments together. On the reading of 'degrees', al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi regard the readings with and without the annexed form as close in meaning, since one whose degree is raised is raised, and one who is raised has his degree raised. Al-Tabari also notes that the verse addresses the Prophet as well, urging him to take Abraham as a model and to be patient with his people.

This passage in Surat al-An'am recounts that God gave Ibrahim Ishaq and then Ya'qub as a grandson, and guided each of them, as well as Nuh before them. It then lists Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa and Harun as descendants, and concludes that this is how God rewards the good-doers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the pronoun in 'from his descendants' refers to Nuh, since he is the nearest antecedent and since Lut and Yunus were not descended from Ibrahim. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan take it to refer to Ibrahim, with Lut included by extension because he was Ibrahim's nephew and believed in him. The commentators agree that the guidance here means guidance to monotheism and prophethood. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir add that it may also mean guidance to Paradise as a reward for good deeds. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi derive from the verse the superiority of prophets over angels. Al-Razi explains that Isma'il is mentioned after Ishaq because the focus is on the prophets of the Children of Israel, and that Muhammad, descended from Isma'il, is not named in this context. The readings of al-Yasa' differ, and al-Qurtubi notes that the single-lam form is the more common. All agree that guidance is a favour God grants to whom He wills, that association with God nullifies deeds, and that these prophets are the models the Prophet is commanded to follow.

This verse states that God guided Zakariya, Yahya, Isa and Ilyas, and that each of them is among the righteous, meaning those who do what is fitting and avoid what is not. Commentators agree that Zakariya is the son of Adhan, Yahya is his son, and Isa is the son of Maryam. Many draw from Isa's mention among the descendants of Ibrahim or Nuh that children of a daughter count as descendants, since Isa had no father and is related only through his mother. On Ilyas the scholars differ. Ibn Ishaq holds that he is Ilyas son of Yasin, of the line of Harun, al-Dahhak says he descended from Ismail, and al-Qutaybi places him in the tribe of Yusha ibn Nun. Ibn Mas'ud said he is Idris, a view al-Tabari and others reject because Idris is the grandfather of Nuh, while the verse links Ilyas to Nuh. Some identify Ilyas with al-Khidr, and some say al-Yasa' is al-Khidr. As for the pronoun in 'and of his descendants', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir refer it to Nuh, while others refer it to Ibrahim; the second view faces the problem of Lut, Ibrahim's nephew, which some resolve by noting that Arabs call the paternal uncle a father. Al-Razi and others read the verse as praise of the prophets and of the excellence of guidance, and several conclude from it that prophets are superior to angels. Ibn Kathir adds that these prophets could never have associated others with God, and some cite the verse to show that the sons of Fatima belong to the Prophet's descendants.

This verse names Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut, whom God guided and whom He preferred over the peoples of their times. The commentators agree that Isma'il is the son of Ibrahim, that Yunus is Jonah son of Matta, and that Lut is Ibrahim's nephew. On al-Yasa', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others say he is the son of Akhtub, son of al-'Ajuz, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report the view that he is Yusha' ibn Nun, and al-Biqa'i takes him to be Ilyas's successor. The readings differ: most read al-Yasa' with a single light lam, whereas Hamza and al-Kisa'i read al-Laysa' with a doubled lam. Al-Tabari prefers the first because the transmitters agree on it, while al-Farra' and al-Makki find the second closer to foreign names. On whether the pronoun in 'his offspring' refers to Nuh or to Ibrahim, al-Farra' and al-Tabari favour Nuh, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and others favour Ibrahim, with Lut included by a broad reckoning of descent. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the phrase 'preferred over the worlds' as proof that prophets are superior, al-Razi even over angels, though most read 'worlds' as the peoples of each prophet's era. All agree the passage lists the blessings given to Ibrahim and that shirk would nullify deeds.

This verse speaks of the favours God bestowed on the prophets mentioned before it, and on some of their fathers, descendants and brothers: God chose them and guided them to the straight path, which most commentators understand as monotheism, the pure faith free from any association with God. The exegetes agree that the particle "min" is partitive, since some of the fathers and descendants were not guided or had no offspring at all. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain the word ijtiba' as choosing and selecting, Mujahid renders it as purifying, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi derive it from gathering water into a basin. As for guidance, al-Razi sometimes takes it to mean the reward of paradise and others take it as the commission to prophethood, but the most common view is guidance to faith and the oneness of God.

The commentators differ on what the pronoun "his descendants" refers to after the mention of Noah: al-Tabari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi take it to refer to Noah, since he is the nearest antecedent and Lot was not a descendant of Abraham, whereas al-Zajjaj and Ata' take it to refer to Abraham. Ibn Kathir and others note that Jesus is counted among Abraham's descendants through his mother, an argument Yahya ibn Ya'mur used against al-Hajjaj.

The sentence "If these people disbelieve in them, We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them" is also read differently: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take the disbelievers to be the people of Mecca and the entrusted people to be the Ansar of Medina, Qatada and al-Hasan take the entrusted ones to be the prophets mentioned, Abu Raja' takes them to be the angels, and Mujahid takes them to be the Persians. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi hold that the verse applies to believers until the Day of Resurrection. As for the command to follow their guidance, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya limit it to the foundations of faith rather than to the laws, which differ from one revelation to another.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to the guidance God granted to the prophets mentioned just before it, a support and grace that He gives to whomever He wills among His servants to lead them to the true religion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand this guidance as the religion of God and monotheism, while al-Razi understands it as reward and entry into Paradise, or as prophethood and messengership, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it to mean what these prophets adhered to. They all agree that guidance depends on God's will and favour, and al-Nasafi notes that the verse refutes the Mu'tazila's claim that God willed the guidance of all creation.

As for the words "and had they associated others with Him, their deeds would have been nullified," the commentators agree that association nullifies good deeds, and that this is a hypothetical statement meant to magnify the gravity of shirk and to warn against it. Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti point out that a conditional does not imply that the condition occurs. Al-Tabari explains "habita" as the loss and disappearance of reward, and al-Zamakhshari as destruction.

Opinions differ on the meaning of the Book, the wisdom and the prophethood. Ibn 'Atiyya understands wisdom as understanding and religious insight, while al-Alusi sees it as judgment between people or wisdom. They also differ on who rejects these gifts: according to Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir they are the people of Mecca, while others identify the people entrusted with them as the Ansar or the people of Medina, al-Hasan and Qatada identify them as the mentioned prophets, Abu Raja' as the angels, and Mujahid as the Persians.

Most commentators hold that the command to follow the guidance of these prophets concerns the foundations of faith and monotheism rather than the particular laws, which differ. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari cite patience and noble character as areas of emulation. The verse ends with the statement that the Prophet asks no wage for the Qur'an, which is a reminder for all the worlds.

This verse refers to the prophets named just before, together with their fathers, descendants and brothers, to whom God gave the Book, judgment and prophethood. It states that if the people of Mecca reject these gifts, God has already entrusted them to another people who will not disbelieve in them. The commentators differ on who the "these" and the "people" are. For "these", most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, mean the disbelievers of Mecca, while Mujahid says the Persians and some say the Prophet's community. For "a people", Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd, Qatada and al-Tabari identify the Ansar of Medina, and al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi include both the Emigrants and the Helpers. Abu Raja al-'Utaridi understands the angels, a view al-Razi considers distant because the word qawm rarely refers to non-humans. Al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Zajjaj take it as the prophets already mentioned, and al-Zajjaj relies on the following verse, "those are the ones God guided, so follow their guidance". Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi adopt this reading. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the wording also includes all believers until the Day of Resurrection. As for the word "entrusted", Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur understand it as God's guiding and enabling a people to hold to faith and fulfil its duties, and al-Alusi speaks of being directed to the faith and its obligations.

The commentators explain that « those whom God guided » are the prophets mentioned just before, and that the command « follow their guidance » is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. Most of them agree that this guidance means monotheism, the foundations of the religion, and patience in the face of hostility, not the specific legal rulings, which differ between communities. Al-Wahidi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi state this clearly. Some scholars, such as al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi and the opinions gathered by al-Qurtubi, hold instead that the command extends to the laws of earlier peoples. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya find this view unconvincing for several reasons, and al-Razi draws from the verse an indication that the Prophet surpassed all earlier prophets, a point taken up by al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di.

On the phrase « if these disbelieve in it », the scholars differ over who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and as-Suddi understand « these » to be the people of Mecca, and the « people » entrusted with the message to be the Ansar of Medina. Mujahid identifies them as the Persians, Abu Raja as the angels, and al-Hasan and Qatada as the prophets and believers. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan note that the verse may apply to all disbelievers and believers until the Day of Resurrection.

As for « I ask of you no reward for it; it is only a reminder to all the worlds », the commentators read it as saying that the Prophet asks no payment for conveying the Quran, which is an admonition for jinn and humankind alike. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi derive from it a prohibition on taking pay for teaching the Quran, while al-Shawkani qualifies this by noting exceptions recognised by jurists, and al-Alusi uses it to affirm the universal scope of the prophetic mission.

In this verse God states that those who deny that revelation was sent to any human did not know God as He deserves to be known nor glorify Him as He should be glorified, saying that God revealed nothing to a mortal. The commentators differ on who said this. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima and Ibn Kathir, and al-Tabari after them, hold that they were the polytheists of Quraysh, who rejected human messengers; al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi understand them to be Jews, and name Malik ibn as-Sayf and Finhas. Those who take the Jews as the target read the following address as directed at them: they turned the Book revealed to Moses into scattered sheets, showing some parts and hiding much, including what concerns the Prophet. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and others note that the reading in the second person, followed by most reciters, differs from the third-person reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr. As for the phrase 'and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew', some take it as addressed to the Jews regarding the Torah, others to the Muslims or Arabs regarding the Quran. The answer 'God' is understood by Ibn Abbas and most scholars as meaning that God sent it down. The command to leave them in their idle talk is seen by some as abrogated by the verses on fighting, while others read it as a threat that needs no abrogation. The verses conclude by describing the Quran as a blessed book confirming earlier scriptures, sent to warn the Mother of Cities and those around her, and say that those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it and keep up their prayers.

This verse states that the Qur'an is a Book God sent down to His Prophet Muhammad, blessed and abundant in good, confirming the Scriptures that came before it. It was revealed to warn the Mother of Towns, Mecca, and those around it. The commentators agree that those who believe in the Last Day also believe in this Book and guard their prayers. Fear of the Hereafter drives a person to reflect until he believes, and care for the prayer is the sign of that faith. There is broad agreement that the Mother of Towns is Mecca, though the reasons for the name differ. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir say the earth was spread out from beneath it, while as-Suddi and most exegetes say it houses the first house built for people. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya describe it as the qibla and gathering place of other towns, and the greatest of them. As for 'those around it', Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the people of the whole earth, while some read it as the Arabs alone; Ibn Kathir and al-Razi reject this, citing verses that establish the message's universality. Commentators also differ on what 'it' refers to in 'believe in it': some say the Book, others the Prophet. The prayer is singled out because it is the pillar of religion and the mark of faith. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi also report that the following verses were revealed concerning Musaylima the liar and Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh.

This verse declares that no one is more unjust than the one who fabricates a lie against God, claiming to be a prophet or to have received a revelation when none was given to him, or boasting that he can send down the like of what God has sent. The commentators then describe the fate of these wrongdoers at the moment of death, when the agonies of death overwhelm them and the angels, stretching out their hands, say: 'Bring out your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the torment of humiliation for what you said against God other than the truth, and for your arrogance toward His signs.' The commentators agree that the verse is general in scope: false prophecy and religious fabrication fall under it, and the individuals named in the reports of revelation, such as Musaylima, al-Aswad al-Ansi, Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, are examples rather than the sole target. They differ on the phrase 'stretching out their hands': Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi take it to mean striking, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take it to mean punishment, and al-Farra' takes it to mean seizing the souls. Ibn Abbas places this at the time of death, whereas al-Hasan places it in the Fire. Lexicographers explain that 'hawn' means humiliation, and some note that the vowelled form with a fatha means gentleness. Ibn Kathir relates that the disbeliever's soul refuses to leave and is struck until it departs. Al-Zamakhshari and others read the 'agonies of death' figuratively for the severity of the ordeal, possibly extending to the torments of the afterlife. Finally, the words 'You have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time' are taken by the commentators as addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, stripped of wealth, helpers and the intercessors they had claimed as partners.

This verse describes the state of the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection, when they are rebuked: you have come to Us alone, with no wealth, family or helpers, just as We created you the first time, bare and without possessions. You have left behind what We had bestowed upon you, and we do not see with you the intercessors you claimed were partners of God and would intercede for you. What bound you together is cut off, and what you used to claim has vanished. The commentators agree that the verse depicts a person stripped of everything he took pride in during this life. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada identify the intercessors as the idols, while Muqatil says they were the angels whose intercession was believed in. Al-Tabari and others report that the verse was revealed about al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said that al-Lat and al-Uzza would intercede for him, and al-Mawardi and others connect the preceding verse to Musaylima and Ibn Abi Sarh. On the reading of «baynakum», al-Tabari holds that the nominative and accusative readings carry the same meaning, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi consider the nominative better, meaning your ties have been severed. Ibn 'Atiyya accepts both readings, reading bayn as either connection or separation. Most exegetes take 'what We bestowed upon you' to mean wealth, children and servants, and read the verse as a reproach to those who boasted of their possessions.

The commentators explain that God splits the seed and the date-stone to bring forth the plant and the tree, a sign of His power that none of those worshipped besides Him can match. They differ on the meaning of "faliq". Al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take it as the split from which the ear of grain emerges from the kernel and the palm from the stone. Mujahid and Abu Malik understand the two fissures that exist within the grain and the stone. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean "creator". Al-Tabari rejects this sense as unattested in Arabic, while al-Zajjaj and al-Fayruzabadi report it. Al-Razi argues that splitting implies bringing into existence, so the splitter may be understood as the Originator.

As for "He brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living", most exegetes read it as the ear emerging from the grain and the palm from the stone, and the reverse. Ibn 'Abbas also gives the sense of the human being produced from a drop and the drop produced from a human, while al-Hasan reads it as the believer brought out of the unbeliever and the reverse. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir hold that the phrase covers both animals and plants, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers this the stronger view. Al-Razi notes that a growing plant counts as living, which explains the parallel construction. The readings also differ on whether "mayyit" is doubled.

The verse concludes that this is Allah, the only one deserving worship, and the question "how then are you turned away?" is a rebuke to those who turn from His oneness.

This verse states that God splits the darkness of night to bring forth dawn, made the night a resting place in which people find calm after the toil of the day, and set the sun and the moon in motion by a precise reckoning by which time is measured. This is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing. The commentators broadly agree on the basic meaning: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that dawn is the light that appears at the end of the night, and that night is a time of rest when every creature withdraws. On the meaning of splitting, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that it may refer to the cleft of dawn through the darkness, or to the separation of light from darkness; al-Razi develops this into an argument that the light of dawn comes from God's direct creation and not from the sun alone. On the word hisban, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it to mean reckoning, while Ibn Abbas understands it as the counting of days, months and years, and Qatada as light, a view al-Tabari finds unconvincing. On the readings, al-Tabari judges the variant forms to be equally valid in meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn see in the pair al-Aziz al-Alim an expression of divine power and knowledge, and al-Razi reads in it proof that these movements are not governed by nature alone but by divine choice. The commentators do not settle between these readings, but all of them see in the verse an invitation to reflect on the order of creation.

In this verse God reminds people of one of His favours: He placed the stars so that you might be guided by them through the darkness of land and sea. Most commentators understand the plain meaning as finding one's way when lost at night. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi, together with Abu Hayyan, take the darknesses to be the darkness of the night, with the phrase about land and sea expressing mere association. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy add that the expression may refer metaphorically to confusing paths. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya extend the sense to the darkness of error and ignorance. Al-Razi presents the verse as evidence of God's power and oneness, and lists further benefits such as fixing the qibla and the prayer times. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di draw from it the permissibility of learning the courses of the stars for this purpose. Ibn Kathir cites early scholars who said the stars serve three ends: adorning the sky, pelting devils, and guidance. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti note that the Quran mentions other functions. Al-Alusi stresses that the stars have no power of their own, and that the prohibitions on astrology concern claims to know the future. The verse closes by saying the signs have been made clear for a people who know, meaning those who benefit from reflecting on them.

This verse states that God brought humanity into being from a single soul, which most commentators identify as Adam, peace be upon him, and that people have two states: a settled place of rest and a temporary place of deposit. The commentators agree that the verse is a proof of God's power, knowledge and wisdom, and that the signs are made clear for those who truly understand. On the meaning of the two terms, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatada and as-Suddi, followed by most scholars, explain that the settled place is the womb and the deposit is the loins of men, a view Ibn Kathir considers the most apparent. Ibn Mas'ud holds the reverse, with the womb as the deposit and the grave as the settled place. Al-Hasan takes the settled place to be the grave and the deposit to be worldly life, while Mujahid places the settled state in this world and the deposit with God in the hereafter. Al-Tabari argues that the verse encompasses all these meanings, since each is a form of settling or depositing, unless an authentic report specifies one. On recitation, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the word with a kasra as an active participle, while the majority read it with a fatha as a noun of place or of verbal noun. The commentators conclude that only those who reflect carefully on the creation of humans benefit fully from these clear signs.

This verse describes God sending down rain from the sky and bringing forth by it every kind of plant: green shoots, then grain piled in ears, clusters of dates hanging low from the palm's spathe, gardens of grapes, olives and pomegranates, some resembling one another and others differing. People are told to look at the fruit as it first appears and as it ripens, a sign for those who believe. Most commentators take the water to be rain and read the word for plant broadly as anything that grows. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the green produce is the tender young crop, and that the layered grain is the ear of corn, a view also given by al-Suddi. Ibn Abbas and al-Bara' understand the close clusters as those within easy reach, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that they are short palms whose bunches hang near the ground. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the nominative reading of the gardens is attested but differs from the common accusative reading, which they explain by an implied verb or a contrast. On the word for fruit, al-Tabari prefers the plural reading that means goods, while Mujahid reads it as wealth. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas understand the ripening as the fruit becoming ripe. Al-Razi discusses the varied qualities of the fruit in detail, and al-Qurtubi gives linguistic and agricultural precision on the stages of ripening. Most commentators conclude that the signs are meant for all, though only believers benefit from them.

This verse condemns those who set up jinn as partners to God, even though He created them, and who attributed sons and daughters to Him without knowledge. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the partnership consisted of obeying the jinn and worshipping them, or of making the angels God's daughters. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the idolaters followed the devils in worshipping idols, and Ibn Kathir supports this with several parallel verses. Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd understand the jinn to be the angels whom some Arabs called God's daughters, a view al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also record. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Razi and others, link the verse to the Zindiq or Magian dualists who held that Good and Evil come from two gods, and al-Razi uses the phrase 'and He created them' to argue against this view. Scholars differ on how to read the verb 'kharraqu', with Nafi' using the doubled form for intensity while most readers use the single form, meaning to invent or fabricate. Al-Hasan says it was an Arabic idiom for telling a lie. The 'sons' refer to Jewish and Christian claims about Ezra and Jesus, and the 'daughters' to the Arab claim about the angels. All agree that these claims are without knowledge, and the verse closes by exalting God above what they describe.

This verse states that God is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, meaning the one who created them without any prior model, and that He cannot have a child, since a child comes only from a spouse and from a being of the same kind as its parent, whereas God creates all things and has neither equal nor spouse. The commentators agree that the verse answers those who attributed sons and daughters to God, such as the idolaters who called the angels God's daughters, the Jews regarding Uzayr, the Christians regarding the Messiah, and those who made the jinn God's associates. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that a child is born of two partners of the same nature, which cannot apply to God. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi give three arguments: the heavens and the earth are God's creatures and cannot be His child; a child must share its parent's nature; and a son would be the equal of his father, while nothing is equal to God. Al-Razi examines the possible meanings of "child" one by one and rejects each, holding that God's knowledge and power of all things leave no need for a son. Ibn 'Ashur sees here an argument from the creation of place and what it contains. As for the phrase "all things", al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean the created world, excluding God's attributes and speech, whereas God's knowledge is understood to encompass everything without restriction. The commentators also discuss variant readings and grammatical analyses of the verse, but these debates do not alter its general meaning.

This verse declares that God alone is the Lord and the only deity, the creator of everything, and therefore that He alone must be worshipped, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain. The commentators agree that creation here means bringing things into existence, and that the wakil is the guardian and manager who provides sustenance, sets the terms of life and watches over deeds. According to al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, the verse answers those who gave God partners among the jinn and ascribed sons and daughters to Him, since a child is born only of a spouse and of the same nature as the father, whereas God is beyond any likeness. Al-Razi argues that oneness is shown because one creator suffices to govern the world, while many would lead to paralysis or conflict, and he notes that the fa in fa'budoohu marks creation as the cause that makes God deserving of worship. On the scope of kull shay' opinions differ: al-Razi, relying on Sunni arguments, takes it as proof that God creates the acts of His servants, whereas the Mu'tazilites he cites hold that human acts are excluded; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi consider that the term is not a general term that has been restricted, since God's attributes are not included in it. Modern commentators such as Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di read in the verse a call to give God the worship due to Him and to entrust Him with one's affairs.

The commentators explain that the verse means that eyes cannot encompass God or grasp the reality of His essence, while He encompasses the eyes with His knowledge, and that He is the Subtle toward His servants, the All-Aware of their affairs. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Zajjaj, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' and Ibn Kathir agree that what is denied is comprehension and complete encompassing, not mere sight, so in their view the verse does not contradict the vision of the believers in the hereafter, which they support with the verse 'faces that day radiant, gazing at their Lord' and with authentic hadiths.

The matter remains disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, in one reported version, al-Ash'ari, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and their followers hold that God will be seen in the hereafter and that the believers will see Him. The Mu'tazilites took the verse as negating any vision, a view answered by al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya, who argue that denying perception does not entail denying sight and that the verse praises God in a way that presupposes vision. 'A'isha maintained that the Prophet did not see his Lord, a position also attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra with variations, while others report that he saw Him with his heart or his eyes.

Some interpreters restrict the negation to worldly life, others hold the verse is general but specified for the believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention the view that God will create for the believers a sixth sense by which they see Him. Al-Zamakhshari reads 'the Subtle' as meaning He eludes sight, and 'the Aware' as knowing all that is subtle; others take subtlety as God's kindness to His servants and knowledge of their interests.

This verse records God's command to His Prophet ﷺ to tell the polytheists that clear proofs, the baṣā'ir by which guidance is distinguished from error and truth from falsehood, have come to them from their Lord in the Qur'an and the revelation. Whoever sees and believes benefits himself, and whoever becomes blind bears the harm of his blindness himself. The Prophet is not a watcher who counts their deeds and repays them; he is a messenger who conveys the message, while God is the Guardian who misses nothing. The commentators agree that the baṣā'ir are proofs and evidences, and that seeing and blindness stand for guidance and misguidance, whose effect returns to the person who acts. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that the words are spoken in the Prophet's own voice, since the verse ends with « I am not a guardian over you ». Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and most exegetes understand 'ḥafīẓ' as a watcher or guarantor who would compel people to believe, and al-Qurtubi and al-Razi report that this belongs to the period before the command to fight. Al-Wahidi, al-Sam'ani and al-Zajjaj hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword; al-Razi finds this thesis too readily accepted and prefers to keep the verse in force, since the Prophet was not charged with counting deeds. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn Sa'di stress human free choice, and al-Qasimi recalls that guidance and error rest on the person's own choice.

This verse states that God varies and repeats His signs in many forms so that the proof becomes clear. The commentators agree on the general meaning: God presents His verses in diverse ways so that the truth is manifest. The reading of the word "darasta" ("you have studied") divides the exegetes. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak read it as "you have read and learned", and al-Tabari considers this the most sound reading, since it matches what the Qur'an reports of the accusation that a human teaches the Prophet. Others read "darasta" with an alif, meaning "you have studied with and disputed against" the People of the Book, as Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr report, and al-Zamakhshari takes it as the Jews studying with the Prophet. Al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read "darasat", meaning that these narratives are ancient and have faded away, while Qatada reads "duristat", meaning they have been recited. Regarding the lam of "liyaqulu", most commentators take it as the lam of consequence: the outcome of this variation is that they say such things, not its purpose. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes it from the lam of "li-nubayyinahu", which he takes as a real purpose. Al-Razi sees in the phrase "for a people who know" a sign that the same unfolding guides some and misleads others. Ibn Kathir links the verse to other passages where the Qur'an guides some and leads others astray.

In this verse God commands His Prophet Muhammad to follow what has been revealed to him from his Lord, to act upon it and to refrain from what it forbids, and to leave aside what the idolaters of his people call him to, namely the worship of idols, since there is no god but Him. As to turning away from the polytheists, most commentators understand it as ceasing to argue and dispute with them and not paying heed to their false claims. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Abbas, holds that this was abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi take turning away to include refraining from fighting, and regard it as a rule from the early days of Islam. Al-Razi notes that not responding in the moment does not imply a permanent prohibition, so abrogation is not required. On the words that if God had willed they would not have associated others with Him, al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas take it to mean that God could have guided them all together, while al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi list several readings: that He could have made them believers, sent a sign compelling them to faith, or destroyed them. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya see the verse as a reply to the Mu'tazilites, al-Razi arguing that the will meant is compulsion. The commentators also address the prohibition on insulting the idols of the polytheists lest they insult God out of ignorance. Ibn Kathir relates that this was prompted by a demand from the Quraysh to Abu Talib, while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Sa'di hold the ruling to remain as long as the unbeliever has protection, since the means to a forbidden act are judged by where they lead.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to follow what is revealed to him and to turn away from the polytheists, and it states that had God willed, He would have prevented them from associating others with Him. The Prophet is not made a guardian over them nor responsible for their affairs; he is only a messenger. On the meaning of "had God willed," the commentators offer closely related explanations: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' take it to mean that God could have gathered them upon guidance, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi that He could have made them believers, and al-Zajjaj reports three possibilities, including sending a sign that would compel their faith or destroying them. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya connect the phrase "there is no god but Him" to the obligation to follow the revelation, whereas al-Zamakhshari treats it as a parenthetical remark with no grammatical role. On turning away, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Razi argues that the command concerns only avoiding confrontation for the time being and need not be considered abrogated. Sunni scholars cite the verse to affirm that God does not will the disbelief-free faith of the unbeliever in the sense of commanding it, while the Mu'tazilis, as al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan report, read the will as compulsion. Ibn Kathir explains that "guardian" means watching over their deeds and provisions, and Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi stress that disbelief is a matter of free choice. The commentators therefore do not agree on a single reading, and God knows best what He intends.

This verse forbids believers from insulting the idols that the polytheists worship besides God, lest the polytheists retaliate by insulting God out of hostility and ignorance. The commentators agree on this basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate, through Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Qatada, that some Muslims cursed the idols and that the Quraysh threatened to curse God in return, and they also report the story of the Quraysh's approach to Abu Talib. Al-Razi and Ibn Attiyya draw a general principle from it: a permissible act that leads to a greater harm must be avoided, a rule that Maliki jurists call blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i). Ibn Ashur holds that the ruling remains valid and is not abrogated, a view shared by al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi argue that an act of obedience which leads to a greater disobedience must be set aside. On the phrase 'We made fair-seeming to every community its deeds', the Sunni scholars such as al-Razi and Ibn Kathir take it as God's action, while the Mu'tazilites such as al-Zamakhshari read it as God leaving people to their choices or as Satan's enticement. Most readers recite 'adwan, while Yaqub, al-Hasan and others read 'udwan. The verse ends with the return to God, when people will be informed of their deeds and judged accordingly.

This verse reports the solemn oaths of the polytheists, who swear by God that they will believe if a sign comes to them. God commands His Prophet to answer that signs belong to God alone, who sends them when He wills, and that they are not in the Prophet's power. The commentators differ on who is addressed by the phrase 'and what would make you aware'. According to Mujahid and Ibn Zayd it addresses the polytheists themselves; according to al-Farra' and others it addresses the believers, who hoped that a sign would bring their unbelieving kin to faith. The majority reading 'annaha' with an open alif has been explained in several ways: al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Farra' take 'anna' to mean 'perhaps', supported by Arabic verses and by the reading attributed to Ubayy; others regard the 'la' as superfluous, a view al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas reject. The reading 'innaha' with a kasra, followed by Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, forms an independent statement that they will not believe when the sign comes. Exegetes report that the Quraysh asked for miracles like those of Moses or Jesus, and that the Prophet, eager for their faith, wished to obtain one; the verse then makes clear that the matter rests with God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi draw from it the lesson of divine wisdom, since God does not send signs that He knows would not lead the demanders to faith.

The commentators explain that the verse describes the idolaters who swore by God with their most solemn oaths that they would believe if a miraculous sign were sent to them. God answers that signs are with Him alone, that He sends them as He wills, and that He knows they will not believe even if the sign comes. Most agree that turning their hearts and sight means diverting them from the truth and preventing them from believing, so that their hearts do not understand and their eyes do not see, just as they did not believe in earlier signs the first time. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Kathir and others. Al-Baghawi understands the earlier signs as miracles such as the splitting of the moon, and Ibn Ashur takes the pronoun to refer to the Quran. As for the 'first time', some place it in this world, at a hypothetical return from the afterlife, as Ibn Abi Talha reports from Ibn Abbas, while others mean the first coming of the signs. Al-Tabari reads the particle 'as' as a comparison with an implied omission, whereas al-Ka'bi and the Mu'tazilites take it as a punishment rather than a direct turning of hearts. Al-Razi argues that the verse shows that belief and disbelief rest on God's decree and rejects the Mu'tazilite readings. Finally, leaving them in their transgression, wandering, means for most that God abandons them to their misguidance: tughyan is excess in evil and 'ama is bewilderment. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse that sins can prevent a good end, and reports that Abu al-Darda recited it on his deathbed.

This verse says that even if God answered the demands of the idolaters by sending down angels to them in plain sight, raising the dead to speak to them, and gathering before them everything they asked for, they would still not believe unless God willed it. The commentators agree on this plain sense but differ on the difficult word "qubulan". Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Tabari, read it as "face to face" or "in plain view", the reading of Nafi and Ibn Amir with a kasra and fatha. The majority reading, with two dammas, has three interpretations: the plural of "qabil" meaning guarantor, as al-Farra and al-Zajjaj hold; the plural of "qabila", meaning groups or kinds, as Mujahid says; or direct confrontation, as Ibn Zayd says. Ibn Kathir and others take it as proof that guidance belongs to God alone. Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazila read the exception as compulsion, which al-Razi answers by distinguishing chosen faith from forced faith. Al-Mawardi reports two possible senses: that God helps them to believe, or that He compels them, a view attributed to al-Hasan al-Basri. As for the closing words, "but most of them are ignorant", al-Tabari explains it as the ignorance of those who think faith depends on their own choice, while al-Mawardi and others see it as ignorance of the fact that they would not believe even if every sign came. Some report that the verse was revealed about the mockers of Quraysh, but al-Tabari favours a general scope, and Ibn Kathir stresses that it consoles the Prophet.

The commentators explain that God consoles His Prophet ﷺ by reminding him that this is a constant practice: He assigned to every prophet enemies among the devils of mankind and the jinn, who inspire one another with ornamented speech full of falsehood in order to deceive people. Most agree that the 'devils' are the rebellious and obstinate of both kinds, as Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir state, and they cite the hadith of Abu Dhar, quoted by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, that there are devils among humans too. Ikrima, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi held instead that each kind has its own devils who meet and inspire one another; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari found this view unsupported. The word 'wahy' means a hidden suggestion, 'zukhruf al-qawl' is embellished and deceptive speech, and 'ghurur' is delusion. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir see in the passage a divine decree behind misguidance, while al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazila read it as God leaving the prophets' enemies free. As for 'Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as a trial that separates believers, while others refer it to the whispering, the disbelief or the deceit. The clause 'that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it' is explained by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi as leaning and approval, and several see in it the result of committing sins. Many exegetes, including al-Nahhas and Ibn Kathir, consider the command 'leave them' abrogated by the verses on fighting, while others read it as turning away with a warning.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the passage about the enemies of the prophets: the devils among men and jinn inspire one another with deceptive, ornamented speech in order to delude the disbelievers. The hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter then incline toward this speech, are pleased with it, and commit the sins they commit. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi explain that « liyaqtarifu » means to gain or to do what they do, al-Tabari taking it to mean acquiring through their deeds, while al-Zajjaj understands it as committing sins. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat the lam as the lam of outcome, meaning that this is the result of such inspiration, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy read it as the lam of purpose, coordinated with « ghurur ». Al-Razi reports that the Mu'tazilites interpreted the lam as an imperative or as a lam of consequence to avoid the idea that God desires disbelief, while the traditional reading takes it literally, and he does not settle the dispute. Ibn Kathir holds that enmity toward the prophets is part of a divine trial and that these devils are the source of the trouble. Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi add that belief in the Hereafter keeps the heart from leaning toward these deceptive words, whereas those who deny it are drawn to them.

God instructs His Prophet to answer those who ask him to accept another judge: shall I seek a judge other than God, who has sent down to you the Book, explained in detail, distinguishing truth from falsehood and the lawful from the unlawful? al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and others explain the verse this way: God is the just judge who rules only by truth. al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that 'hakam' is stronger than 'hakim', since it is applied only to one who is just, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the Kharijites used this verse against 'Ali to condemn arbitration, an argument he finds unsound. As for those who were given the Book, the commentators differ. The majority, including al-Mawardi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, take them to be the learned Jews and Christians who recognise that the Qur'an is sent down from their Lord, in agreement with what they have. al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi also report that they may be believers among the People of the Book, while 'Ata' understood them as the leading Companions such as Abu Bakr and 'Umar. Readers differ on 'munazzal': Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read it with doubling, the others without. On the prohibition against doubt, most commentators see it as an exhortation and encouragement addressed to the Prophet, while others address every listener or the community. Finally, the phrase 'the word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice' means, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, that God's reports are true and His commands just, and that none can alter His words.

The commentators explain that the plain meaning of the verse is that God's word, meaning the revelation He sent down, has been completed in its truthfulness and justice, so no one can change or annul it. They differ on what the word refers to. Qatada and most exegetes, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean the Quran, while others, such as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it to mean God's decrees, promises and rulings. As for its completion, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur understand it as reaching perfection in truthfulness and justice, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as the word continuing and taking effect, and he criticises al-Tabari's view that the words truthful and just are specifications.

The commentators broadly agree that truthfulness concerns reports, promises and threats, and that justice concerns commands and prohibitions, though they order these differently. Most read the statement that no one can alter His words as a prohibition on any corruption, whether by addition, omission or distortion. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir apply it to the Jews and Christians who altered their scriptures, al-Qurtubi and al-Suyuti see in it evidence that the Quran is preserved, and Ibn 'Atiyya allows that alteration may happen through interpretation, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Alusi also cites Abu Muslim, who takes the word to mean God's religion.

The verse ends by affirming that God hears His servants' words and knows their states. Al-Razi uses this to argue for an unchangeable divine decree, a point al-Alusi discusses and disputes. In its context, the verse tells the Prophet to take God alone as judge and warns that following the majority on earth leads astray from God's path.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ not to obey most of those on earth, for obeying them would lead him astray from God's path, since they follow only conjecture and merely guess. The commentators agree that "most of those on earth" refers to the disbelievers, who were the majority at that time, and that one who is astray only commands what leads to error. On the meaning of "earth", Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the whole world, while al-Baydawi and others take it to be the land of Mecca alone. On the "conjecture", al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari understand it as the unbelievers' assumption that their forefathers were right, which they simply imitate. Ar-Razi reads it as the claim of those who dispute with the Prophet that they hold their views without certainty, and Abu Hayyan notes that their beliefs are not based on knowledge. As for the verb "kharasa", most explain it as lying or rough estimation without certainty, like someone guessing the yield of a date palm by eye. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti point out that the context condemns reasoning built on illusory indications more than outright lying. Several accounts of the occasion of revelation are given, the most cited being the dispute over eating animals that died without slaughter, recorded by al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi. Ar-Razi draws from the verse an argument against analogical reasoning (qiyas), which other scholars reject. Ibn Sa'di concludes that truth is not recognised by the number of its followers, a point most exegetes accept from the context.

This verse tells the Prophet, peace be upon him, that his Lord knows best who strays from His path, and that He knows best who is rightly guided. Al-Tabari explains it as a warning against obeying the idolaters, who might lead him astray with ornate speech inspired by devils, since God knows better than anyone, including the Prophet, who is misled and who is upright. Most commentators read it as an affirmation that God perfectly discerns both groups. Ibn Kathir adds that most people on earth are in error, following conjecture and baseless assumptions, and that God guides or leaves astray whom He wills. Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud see it as a confirmation of the warning in the preceding verse, so that the reader does not become one of the misguided. Ibn Ashur notes that the verse restricts this knowledge exclusively to God and presents the Prophet's guidance as the true path. The grammar is discussed at length. Al-Tabari and al-Farra take (man) as a nominative meaning (which one), while al-Akhfash treats it as a genitive with an implied preposition. Al-Tabari rejects the view that (a'lam) means (ya'lam), because the preposition before (al-muhtadin) argues against it. Al-Razi explains that God's knowledge does not vary, and that the verse emphasizes that God's concern with showing guidance exceeds His concern with showing error. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya connect the passage to the dispute about slaughtered animals. Ibn Sa'di draws the lesson that truth is not measured by the number of its followers.

In this verse God commands the believers to eat what has been slaughtered with the name of God pronounced over it, and makes this obedience a sign of belief in His signs. Most commentators read it as a permission to eat what is slaughtered in God's name alone: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that it means what is slaughtered invoking God and not the names of idols, or what dies naturally. 'Ata', as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya, extends the command to pronouncing God's name over drink, food and slaughter. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi link the verse to what precedes it, the prohibition of following those who declare the forbidden lawful and the lawful forbidden, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the conditional phrase serves as an incitement. The precise meaning of invoking the name divides scholars: al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss the case of forgetting, while al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur hold that the verse does not directly address forgetting the invocation at slaughter, its purpose being to distinguish the permitted from the prohibited. The commentators agree that the verse urges adherence to what God has allowed rather than the customs of idolaters, that the following verse states the lawful and unlawful have been clearly explained, that necessity permits what is otherwise forbidden, and that those who mislead by their desires without knowledge are transgressors whom God will judge.

This verse states that nothing should prevent believers from eating what has been slaughtered with the name of God pronounced over it, since God has clearly explained what He has forbidden to them. They should not refuse what is lawful out of fear of falling into what is unlawful, except in cases of compelling necessity. The commentators agree that the verse permits eating animals slaughtered in God's name, and excludes carrion or what was dedicated to other than God, as Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain. They differ on what the "explanation" refers to. Most, including al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, take it to mean the prohibitions stated in Surat al-Ma'ida, while others note that al-Ma'ida is Medinan and al-An'am Meccan, and prefer the next verse, "I find in what has been revealed to me nothing forbidden…". Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur report that the occasion of revelation was the polytheists' dispute with the Muslims, who were told they ate what they killed themselves but not what God killed. On the phrase about misleading others, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it to mean that they lead others astray, and al-Tabari prefers that reading, while others read it as going astray themselves. Al-Razi draws from it that following others without evidence is blameworthy. The verse ends with a warning to those who transgress from the truth into falsehood.

This verse tells believers to abandon sin both openly and in secret, and then declares that those who earn sin will be repaid for what they have committed. The commentators broadly agree that it is a general call to avoid every disobedience, whether public or hidden. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi keep this wide meaning, and Ibn Kathir adds that it covers both deeds and inner intentions. Qatada understands the outward and inward sin as the open and the secret, Mujahid as bodily acts and what the heart intends, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi repeat this split between what is done and what is willed. Others read it more narrowly. Ibn Zayd, reported by al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, takes the outward sin to be going naked while circling the Kaaba and the inward one to be adultery. Said ibn Jubayr, followed by several scholars, takes it as marriage to forbidden kin and adultery, while al-Suddi and al-Dahhak report that the pre-Islamic Arabs considered secret fornication permitted. Al-Tabari judges these narrower readings to be unsupported without proof. Ibn Sa'di stresses that one must know the sins of the heart in order to avoid them, and Ibn Ashur sees the phrase as a generalisation covering every kind of transgression. Al-Qasimi notes that the Arabic word iqtiraf usually means acquiring something blameworthy, which fits the warning about sin.

This verse forbids believers to eat what has not had God's name pronounced over it at slaughter, calling it a transgression and a departure from obedience. It adds that the devils inspire their allies among the polytheists to dispute with the believers, and that obeying them in this amounts to associating partners with God. The commentators differ on what the phrase refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Mujahid mention carrion or animals sacrificed to idols. Al-Tabari holds that it covers what was offered to idols and what died or was slaughtered by someone whose slaughter is not lawful, and rejects the view that it means a Muslim's animal over which he forgot to say the invocation. On the devils, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn Kathir identify them as jinn devils, while 'Ikrima says they are the Magian rebels of Persia. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari report that the polytheists told the Muslims that they eat what they kill but not what God kills. Scholars disagree on the ruling for an animal slaughtered by a Muslim who omitted the invocation. Al-Shafi'i and his followers permit it whether the omission was forgetful or deliberate. Abu Hanifa, Malik and Ahmad in the prevailing view distinguish forgetting, which is permitted, from deliberate omission, which is forbidden. Dawud, Ibn Sirin and others forbid it in every case. Most commentators take the pronoun in 'and it is perversion' to refer to the act of eating, while al-Zamakhshari allows that it refers to the food. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi hold that obeying the polytheists in lawful and unlawful matters amounts to shirk. Al-Ka'bi takes this as proof that faith covers all acts of obedience, while al-Razi suggests that shirk here may mean believing in a partner in legislation and obligation.

This verse compares the believer whom God guided after straying to a dead man whom God brought to life and gave a light to walk among people, and it sets against him the disbeliever who is in darkness and cannot find a way out. The commentators agree that death, life, light and darkness are images for disbelief, faith, guidance and error, and that the verse covers every believer and every disbeliever, although some reports name particular men. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd take the light to be Islam or the Quran, al-Hasan says it is the Quran, and others say knowledge or faith. Al-Razi understands life as the soul's readiness to receive knowledge and the light as revelation, while Ibn al-Qayyim treats ignorance as a death of the heart and knowledge as its life. The reports of occasion name Hamza and Abu Jahl, or Umar and Abu Jahl, or Ammar and Abu Jahl, but most scholars hold that the wording is general and not limited to the cause. On the phrase 'thus was made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do', the commentators agree that the disbelievers are the ones adorned with their deeds but differ on who does the adorning: al-Hasan and many Mu'tazilites say Satan, al-Razi and the Sunni scholars say God, while al-Zamakhshari allows either and others point to the leaders of the people. Many scholars link the verse to the warning against obeying the polytheists just before it, showing how far apart the two states are.

This verse states a constant divine pattern: in every town Allah places its great and criminal leaders, who plot and scheme against its people. The commentators explain that the "great ones" (akabir) are the chiefs, the notables and the privileged, and that they are singled out because they are the most able to corrupt and lead others astray, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note. Most read "makr" as deception and scheming that turns people away from faith, through deceitful speech and action. Mujahid reports that the Quraysh posted four men on the roads to Mecca to keep travellers from the Prophet ﷺ. All agree that the harm of the scheme falls back on its authors, who do not perceive it because of their deep ignorance, and that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ with a promise of victory. Grammarians differ on how to parse "akabir mujrimiha": some take "akabir" as the first object and "mujrimiha" as a genitive, others reverse the roles, and Abu Hayyan criticises the second reading as contrary to the rule governing the comparative form, while others defend it. Al-Razi and al-Tabari observe that the lam in "liyamkuru" may indicate purpose or consequence; the Mu'tazilites read it as consequence to avoid attributing the scheming to God's will, whereas the Sunnis take it literally as purpose. Some report a occasion of revelation involving al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Abu Jahl, who claimed prophethood for themselves; Ibn Kathir holds that the following verse answers this, since God knows where to place His message. Overall the general meaning is agreed, and the disagreements concern mainly grammar and the context of revelation.

This verse reports that proud leaders of Mecca declared they would not believe until they were given what the messengers of God had been given. The commentators differ on what this demand meant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as a request for tangible miracles such as the parting of the sea or the raising of the dead, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj say they wanted revelation and the angel Gabriel to come to them. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi judge the first view stronger, holding that they sought prophethood itself, a position supported by reports about Abu Jahl and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. God's reply that He knows best where to place His message is accepted by all, though they differ on the grammar of 'haythu': al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it as an object, while al-Zajjaj reads it as a figurative place adverb. The word 'sagar' means humiliation and abasement. Abu Raq and Ibn Kathir say it refers to disgrace in this world, with the severe punishment in the next, whereas others place both in the Hereafter. Al-Farra' reads 'inda Allah' as 'from God', while the Basran grammarians see it as expressing permanence. The word 'makr' means scheming and deceit, and its harm returns to those who practise it.

This verse states God's law of guidance and misguidance: whoever God wants to guide has his breast opened to Islam, while whoever He wants to lead astray has his breast made tight and constricted, as if he were straining to climb into the sky. The commentators agree that guidance and misguidance rest with God's will, that opening the breast means preparing the heart to receive faith, and that tightness and constriction describe its refusal to accept it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith in which the Prophet describes a light cast into the heart, whose signs are turning toward the eternal abode, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death; yet Mahmud Shakir, in his note on al-Tabari, judged most of its chains weak, while al-Shawkani considered them strengthening one another. The word haraj is read with kasra by Nafi' and Abu Bakr and with fatha by the rest, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi treat the two as equivalent. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report 'Umar asking a Bedouin what a haraja is, and the answer, a thicket so dense that no herd or beast can reach it, which 'Umar applied to the disbeliever's heart. On yassa'ad, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take it to mean a painful striving, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj read it as the impossibility of faith, like climbing to heaven. On rijs, Mujahid says it is anything without good, Ibn 'Abbas says it is the devil, Ibn Zayd says it is punishment, and al-Zajjaj says it is curse in this world and torment in the next. Sunni scholars take the verse as proof that guidance and misguidance come from God, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as divine aid and abandonment, a view answered by al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to the path God has laid out for His servants, a straight way without crookedness that leads to His pleasure. They differ on what "this" refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi take it to be Islam, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Qur'an, and Ibn al-Jawzi also records the view that it means monotheism. Al-Razi holds that the closest antecedent is most convincing, namely what the previous verse established: that guidance and misguidance rest on God's decree and creation. All agree that "straight" is an emphatic qualifier, that the signs have been explained in detail, that the address is to the Prophet, and that the remembrance meant is the intellect reflecting on what it contains. It is those who reflect who benefit. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan connect the verse to the preceding discussion of guidance and misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari reads the opening of the breast as divine grace, an interpretation that Sunni commentators take in its plain sense. As for "the abode of peace", most identify it with Paradise, some regard al-Salam as a divine name whose abode it is, and others understand it as the home of safety from every harm. Ibn Sa'di explains that it bears this name because it is free from every defect and distress. Most commentators draw no legal rulings from this verse.

The commentators explain that the verse "For them is the abode of peace with their Lord" promises the Garden to those who reflect on God's signs and take heed from them. "He is their Protector" means, in their view, that God supports them and guides them in this world and rewards them in the next, because of their good deeds. Most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand "the abode of peace" as the Garden, the house of God, al-Salam being one of His names, so that it is attributed to Him in honour. Al-Zajjaj and those who follow him take peace in the sense of safety, a place where no harm ever reaches. Ibn Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan also mention the sense of greeting, since the people of the Garden greet one another in peace, a point supported by al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi, who cite many verses linking the state of the blessed with peace. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that these meanings do not contradict one another. As for "with their Lord", most read it as a guarantee and a secured reward, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Ashur take it as nearness of rank rather than of place, and Abu Hayyan mentions divine hospitality. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl reads "He is their Protector" as help in this life and reward in the next, while al-Razi sees in it God's closeness to His servants, the highest of ranks.

Most commentators describe the Day of Resurrection when God gathers jinn and humans together. He addresses the devils, saying they have led many humans astray, and their human allies reply that each side benefited from the other and that they have reached the term appointed for them. The divine answer declares the Fire their abode, where they will remain forever. The commentators agree that the verse carries rebuke, regret and an admission of guilt. They differ, however, on what the mutual benefit was. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj explain it as humans seeking refuge with the lords of the jinn in valleys, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj take it to mean human obedience to the jinn and the jinn's enticing of humans to desires and sins. The appointed term is death for al-Suddi and al-Hasan, and for others the resurrection. On the exception "save what God wills", opinions vary: Ibn 'Abbas applies it to people whom God knew would later believe; others place it between the resurrection and entry into Hell, or read it as an increase in punishment or a transfer to the bitter cold of zamharir, while al-Tabari takes it to refer to sinners among the monotheists. Ibn 'Atiyya questions the claimed consensus on the eternal punishment of disbelievers. The verse closes by affirming that your Lord is wise and all-knowing.

This verse describes a divine pattern concerning wrongdoers: God lets some of them become allies of others because of what they have earned. The commentators give several related readings of the verb nuwalli. Al-Tabari, who prefers this view, follows Qatada in saying that God makes the wrongdoers allies of one another in disbelief and disobedience, a reading also adopted by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, who add that they will be companions in punishment as they were in this world. Another reading, transmitted from Qatada through Ma'mar, is that they will follow one another into the Fire, which Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir also record.
