Ibn Zayd holds that God empowers some wrongdoers over others, and Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan draw from this a warning that whoever does not stop oppressing will be overpowered by another oppressor. Al-Mawardi and Abu Hayyan also mention the sense of leaving them to one another without help. The particle bima marks cause, namely the sins and disbelief they have earned. Al-Razi links the verse to the kinship between jinn and humans, arguing that like souls gather with like. Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn 'Abbas, reports that when God wills good for a people He appoints their best, and when He wills evil He appoints their worst. Some cite the hadith that whoever helps an oppressor will be given power over by God, though its soundness is disputed. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur mainly read the verse as an admonition not to rely on oppressive rulers.

On the Day of Resurrection, God addresses the assembly of jinn and humans in a rebuke: did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, reciting My signs and warning you of the meeting of this day? They answer that they bear witness against themselves, and that the worldly life deceived them, so they testify to their own disbelief. The commentators agree that the verse is a rebuke and a proof that leaves them no excuse, and that their admission is compelled, since they have no way to deny it. On whether messengers were sent to the jinn, al-Tabari, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and Abu Sulayman, as reported by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, hold that God sent messengers from among the jinn as He sent them from among humans, relying on the apparent wording. Others, including Ibn Jurayj, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, say the messengers were only human, and that the plural covers both groups, as in the verse about pearls and coral coming out of both seas. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that the jinn had only warners (nudhur), those who heard the Qur'an and passed it on to their people. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain the repetition of the testimony: the first time reports their words, the second rebukes them and warns listeners. Some commentators note that this testimony seems to contradict their denial elsewhere, and answer that it differs across the many stages of the Day, or that their limbs are the witnesses.

This verse explains that the sending of messengers reflects God's justice and mercy: He does not destroy the towns for their wrongdoing while their people are heedless and no warning has reached them. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, understand the wrongdoing as polytheism and disbelief, so that God does not punish until He sends messengers to set out His proofs and warn of His punishment on the Day of return. Al-Tabari judges this reading the most sound. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy also report a second reading in which God would not be unjust, but the wrongdoing is that of people destroyed before any warning. Several scholars read heedlessness as lack of awakening rather than deliberate neglect, and al-Razi notes it means God has not clarified their situation or removed their excuse. Al-Razi draws from the verse that obligation does not arise before revelation, a view held by the Sunni scholars he follows, whereas the Mu'tazilites read it as supporting the opposite position. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti stress the general principle that God does not destroy any people without first warning them. On the following verse, most commentators explain that each doer has ranks according to his deeds, and al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir add that these ranks may also refer to degrees of punishment in the Fire. Ibn Kathir notes Ibn 'Amir's reading with the second person in place of the third.

This verse states that every accountable being, whether jinn or human, receives degrees according to what they did: good deeds bring good reward and evil deeds bring a proportionate punishment. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the degrees are ranks of recompense, and that God does not overlook what people do, but records it and will repay them on the day they meet Him. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya connect the verse to the preceding passage on the sending of messengers, since God does not destroy a town unjustly before its people have been warned. Al-Mawardi gives two readings of the injustice, either punishment without warning or the wrongdoing of the people themselves.

The commentators differ on the scope of the verse. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi take it to cover both the obedient and the disobedient, though al-Razi argues that the word degrees fits only the obedient and that the closing clause concerns the rebellious. From the verse, Abu Hanifa concluded that jinn have no reward, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, relying on its general wording, held that they do. Ibn Kathir also suggests that the verse may refer to the unbelievers among jinn and humans, each receiving a degree of punishment in the Fire. Al-Sha'rawi links the differences in rank to sincerity and to extra voluntary acts of worship.

Ibn Ashur notes that degrees are steps of ascent, while lower levels are called depths, and that the word degrees is used here to give good news to the believers. Ibn Amir reads the verb in the second person, while the other readers use the third person.

The commentators explain that God is self-sufficient and free of need from His creatures and their worship, yet He is also full of mercy toward them. Their obedience does not benefit Him and their disobedience does not harm Him; if He imposes duties, rewards, or punishes, it is out of compassion and grace. The verse then states that He could remove them and bring forth others, just as He produced them from the offspring of earlier peoples. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi all read this as a warning to wrongdoers and a demonstration of divine power. They agree that self-sufficiency is an essential attribute of God. As for the addressees, Ibn 'Abbas and others say they are the people of Mecca, 'Ata' says the Companions and Successors, and Muqatil and al-Zamakhshari identify the other people as the people of Noah's ark. Al-Tabari reads the word 'min' as meaning substitution, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it as partitive or as a starting point.

On the statement that what you are promised will certainly come, most read it as the Resurrection and the Gathering, while al-Razi also includes the promise of reward. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri on this point. Regarding 'act according to your standing,' the commentators give several senses, including state, path, position and place, and all agree it is a threat rather than permission. Most understand the 'final abode' as Paradise or victory in this world. The verse ends by affirming that wrongdoers will not prosper.

The commentators explain that this verse warns the polytheists that what they have been promised, whether punishment or resurrection, will certainly come to pass, and that they cannot escape God by fleeing across the earth. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a threat of punishment for persisting in disbelief, and al-Tabari specifies that the address is to the Quraysh. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan take "makanatikum" to mean your side or your place, while al-Mawardi lists several senses: way, condition, position, standing and situation.

Most agree that "mu'jizin" means not being out of reach or escaping. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note that death will overtake them wherever they are. As to what is promised, al-Hasan links it to the coming of the Hour, while al-Razi argues that the word "wa'd" applies chiefly to reward, so the firmness of the statement is stronger for good than for punishment, and mercy predominates. Ibn 'Ashur sees the sentence as an answer to the unbelievers who argued that the punishment was delayed.

The verse follows the passage on God's self-sufficiency and mercy, and his power to remove people and replace them with others. Ibn Kathir cites this replacement as a sign of power, while Ibn Sa'di stresses that this world is a passage, not a dwelling. The verse ends with the command to the Prophet to tell his people to act according to their way while he acts according to his, and that they will know who will have the good outcome of the abode, since wrongdoers never succeed.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to his idolatrous people: act according to your standing, and I am acting too, and you will soon know who will have the good outcome of the abode, for the wrongdoers do not succeed. The commentators agree that the imperative is a threat rather than a permission, like the verse saying do what you will. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that makana means one's state or manner, and Ibn 'Abbas glossed it as one's direction. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite the meaning of established power in this world. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take the good outcome to be the Garden, or, as Ibn 'Atiyya allows, the victory and dominance of this world, which would make the verse a prediction. Al-Tabari prefers reading the interrogative man as the subject, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi give both readings. For Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, the wrongdoers are the disbelievers, and not succeeding means not being saved or winning. Al-Zamakhshari praises the fair tone of the warning, which leaves the outcome to God. Ibn Kathir recalls that the message later prevailed across Arabia and beyond. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i with the letter ya gives the masculin form.

This verse describes a custom of the pagan Arabs, who set aside a portion of their crops and livestock for God and another portion for their idols, saying of the first that it was God's "by their claim" and of the second that it belonged to their associates. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, agree that the closing rebuke, "Evil is their judgment," condemns this unjust division that favoured the idols over God. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi relate concrete examples: when wind or water carried produce from God's portion into the idols' portion they left it there, but when it moved the other way they took it back, justifying this by saying that God is rich and the idols are poor. In years of famine they ate from God's portion and left the idols' portion untouched.

Al-Tabari judges this the most convincing reading, since naming a portion alone does not separate mixed goods. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi report that they compensated losses to the idols' share from God's share but never the reverse. Ibn Zayd understands the matter as one of invocation: they named the idols over what was slaughtered for God, and did not name God over what was slaughtered for the idols. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the blame as aimed at preferring the idols and at practices God had never prescribed. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan debate the grammar of "sa'a," which functions like "bi'sa," and disagree about whether "ma" is a relative pronoun or a specifier.

This verse tells us that many polytheists saw the killing of their children made attractive to them by their associates. The commentators mostly understand this as the burying of baby girls alive out of fear of poverty or shame, and sometimes as sacrificing children to idols. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi say the associates were devils who urged such acts. Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Hasan agree they were devils, al-Kalbi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi say they were the keepers of the idols, and al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi also report that they were misguided people. The purpose of this enticement is given as destruction and confusing their religion. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur read the phrase about destruction as describing the outcome, not the intention, while al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi read it as a purpose. Most take the phrase about God's will as meaning that everything happens by His will, though al-Zamakhshari reads it as His compelling will, a view that Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan reject. The readings also differ: the majority read the associates as the subject, while Ibn Amir reads the killing as the subject with the associates in the genitive, which al-Zamakhshari rejects as flawed but Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and al-Nasir defend as transmitted. The verse ends by telling the Prophet to leave them to their fabrications, which most take as a warning rather than permission.

In this verse God describes what the polytheists claimed: some of their livestock and crops were declared forbidden on their own initiative, without any permission from God. They set aside part of the harvest and cattle for their idols and said that no one could eat from it except those they chose, namely the idols' attendants and men but not women, according to their own claims. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the word hijr means forbidden, and that the livestock and crops refer to what they had dedicated to God and to their idols, though the details of this dedication vary. The commentators agree on two other categories: animals whose backs were forbidden to be ridden or loaded, such as the bahira, sa'iba and hami according to as-Suddi and Mujahid, and animals over which the name of God was not pronounced at slaughter but the names of idols were. Abu Wa'il adds that these were not ridden on pilgrimage. Al-Mawardi and others report several opinions without preferring one over another. The readings of hijr vary between a kasra, a damma and the reading hirj attributed to Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Tabari favours the kasra, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya consider these forms to share the same meaning. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the prohibition on riding certain animals a practice based on a vow. The verse calls their conduct a fabrication against God: al-Tabari explains that they attributed their own prohibition to God, and Ibn Kathir notes that they ascribed it to God's religion without any permission from Him. The verse closes with a warning that they will be recompensed for what they fabricated.

This part of the verse describes another false ruling the pagans made about certain livestock. They claimed that what is in the bellies of these animals, namely the bahira and sa'iba, is reserved for males alone if it is born alive, while if it is born dead, both men and women may share it. Most commentators understand the phrase to refer to the unborn young of these animals. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Sha'bi, however, take it to mean the milk, al-Suddi and Mujahid take it to mean the foetuses, and al-Tabari concludes that the wording covers both. On the word for wives, Mujahid, as reported by al-Tabari, says it means women in general, while Ibn Zayd says it means daughters. The scholars also discuss several recitations and grammatical points. They explain that the feminine form of 'pure' (khalisa) agrees with the sense of the word 'what', that the feminine ending may intensify the meaning as in 'scholar' or 'genealogist', and that the reading of 'dead' varies between the canonical readers. The verse closes with a warning to those who invent lies against God. The commentators explain that the 'description' refers to their false claims about what is lawful and unlawful, and that God is wise in how He repays them and knowing of their deeds.

This verse states that those who killed their children, meaning they buried their daughters alive, out of folly and without knowledge, and who forbade what God had provided them, have lost and gone astray. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this loss covers both this world, through the loss of children and goods, and the next, because of their lying about God. Al-Tabari reports that the verse concerns Rabi'a and Mudar who practised burying daughters, from fear of captivity and poverty, according to 'Ikrima and Qatada, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan note that the Banu Kinana did not do this. As for the prohibition, most commentators link it to the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the hami. The word 'safahan' is glossed as ignorance and levity, and al-Zajjaj treats it as an accusative of purpose or a state. Al-Razi counts seven successive elements: the killing of the child, folly, lack of knowledge, the prohibition of goods, fabrication against God, error, and the absence of guidance. Al-Tabari reports that Abu Razin took 'they have gone astray' to refer to an error that came before these acts, while others take it as their result. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani note that 'they were not guided' may mean they were never guided. Ibn Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb draw a warning against religious innovation, and al-Jaza'iri against legislating without divine permission.

This verse reminds that God brought forth gardens, some trained on trellises like vines and others spreading on the ground, along with palms and crops of varied fruit and taste, and the olive and pomegranate, similar in appearance but different in taste. He permits eating from their fruit when it bears and commands giving its due on the day of harvest, while forbidding excess. The commentators agree on the permission to eat and on the verse's reminder of God's favours. As to the due mentioned, Ibn Abbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and Malik take it to be the obligatory zakat, a tenth or half a tenth. Ali ibn al-Husayn, 'Ata', Mujahid, Hammad, al-Hakam and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to be a right besides zakat, recommended, such as a handful given to the poor present at the harvest. Others hold that it was an obligation later abrogated by zakat, a view reported from Ibn Abbas, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and 'Atiyya, and favoured by al-Tabari. Ibn Kathir finds the term abrogation questionable, since zakat only specified an existing duty. On excess, most read it as giving away all one's wealth so that nothing remains for one's family, as in the case of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas; Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab reads it as withholding alms, al-Zuhri as spending in disobedience, and Ibn Zayd as a warning to rulers against taking more than their due. Al-Tabari considers it best to take all meanings of excess together.

This verse states that God created from the livestock both those used for carrying loads and those too small to carry, then commands people to eat from what He has provided and forbids following the steps of Satan in declaring lawful or unlawful what they invent. The commentators agree on the general sense but differ on the meaning of hamula and farsh. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas in one report, al-Hasan and Mujahid take hamula as the large camels that are ridden or loaded and farsh as the young camels that are not, and al-Tabari chooses this view as the most sound. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Qatada hold that hamula means camels and cattle and farsh means sheep and goats. Ibn Zayd explains hamula as what is ridden and farsh as what is eaten and milked. Ibn Abbas in another report includes horses, mules and donkeys under hamula. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir note that farsh may also refer to cloth woven from wool, hair and fleece. As for following Satan's steps, most read it as the invented prohibitions of the pagan Arabs, while Ibn Zayd reads it as sins and obedience to the wicked. All agree that Satan is a manifest enemy, and al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi recall that he expelled Adam from Paradise. According to al-Razi and al-Nasafi, the verses that follow refute the polytheists' prohibition of certain animals.

This verse states that God created eight kinds of livestock in pairs: two of sheep (ram and ewe), two of goats (billy and nanny), two of camels and two of cattle. For the Arabs, a 'pair' means one animal together with another of its kind. The commentators read the verse as a rebuttal of the idolaters who forbade certain animals such as the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham. God tells His Prophet to ask them whether God forbade the males, the females, or what the wombs of the females contain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read this as a challenge that exposes their claims: any prohibition they assert would logically forbid all males, all females, or every offspring, which they do not accept. Ibn 'Atiyya and the Jalalayn take the question as one of reproach and rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari understands it as a denial that God forbade any of these categories, while al-Razi notes that the division-and-examination argument can also reach other grounds of prohibition beyond sex, such as the bahira or sa'iba. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari and al-Suyuti, says the verse was revealed when Malik ibn 'Awf questioned the Prophet, who silenced him with the argument. The commentators agree that God forbade none of these, that the demand for knowledge and proof is directed at the polytheists, and that attributing such rulings to God is a fabrication. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi name 'Amr ibn Luhayy as the first to introduce these practices.

This verse lists the four kinds of livestock, camels, cattle, sheep and goats, male and female, and refutes the prohibitions the pagan Arabs placed on some of them, such as the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham, along with what their wombs carried. Al-Tabari, al-Samani, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Qasimi read God as asking whether He forbade the males, the females, or what the females carry. If He had forbidden all males, all females, or all offspring, the ruling would have to apply universally, which it does not. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed when Awf or Malik ibn Awf challenged the Prophet.

The commentators agree that the interrogative form is rebuking. The phrase "Were you witnesses?" means that they neither saw God command this prohibition nor believed in a messenger who would relay it. Al-Razi reads the passage as an argument by division and considers its force limited, since a prohibition may rest on other grounds than sex, yet he affirms that fabricating a lie against God is the greatest wrong. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi identify the one who invents lies about God as the most unjust of people, and Ibn Kathir names 'Amr ibn Luhayy first.

On the purpose of the lie, al-Tabari and al-Jalalayn say it is to lead people astray, while Ibn Ashur allows that the lam may indicate consequence. On guidance, most read the closing clause as meaning that God does not guide wrongdoers. Al-Razi and al-Qadi take this as withholding reward, al-Tabari as withholding right direction, and Ibn Ashur notes that many polytheists were later guided after embracing Islam.

This verse tells the Prophet to reject the prohibitions the pagans had invented on their own. He says he finds in what was revealed to him no prohibition on the eater except carrion, flowing blood, pork, which is impure, and what was slaughtered for other than God, which is a transgression. The commentators note that it was revealed in Mecca, before the additions made in Surat al-Ma'ida and the Sunna. Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha and Malik held that the prohibition is limited to these items, while most scholars, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, held that the Sunna extended the prohibitions, for example to predatory animals with fangs, birds with talons and domestic donkeys. On blood, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Abu Majlaz held that only blood that flows is forbidden, not what remains in the veins or mixed with meat, and the Sunna permitted liver and spleen. Whoever is forced by necessity, neither rebellious nor transgressing, is forgiven. The verse also mentions the prohibitions placed on the Jews as punishment for their wrongdoing, including animals with undivided hooves and certain fats of cattle and sheep.

This verse states that God forbade to the Jews certain specific things. The first mentioned is every animal with a claw or hoof, which the commentators largely understand as animals whose toes are not split, such as the camel, ostrich, goose and duck. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Sudi hold this view, while Ibn Zayd restricts it to the camel alone. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi also report that some took it to mean any animal with talons or hooves, in a figurative sense. Regarding the fat of cattle and sheep, Qatada limits it to the fat of the intestines, Ibn Jurayj takes it as all fat not attached to a bone, and al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd include the kidney fat. All agree that the fat on the back and flanks was permitted, and most include the entrails, called al-hawaya, and fat attached to bone, such as the tail fat, among what is excepted. Many cite the authentic hadith in which the Prophet cursed the Jews for melting the forbidden fat and selling it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari explain that the prohibition was a punishment for their wrongdoing, and it serves to refute their claim that Israel alone had forbidden these foods to himself. Ibn al-Arabi and al-Qurtubi note that this ruling was abrogated in Islam, and jurists differ on whether the fat of the slaughter of People of the Book is permitted.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ that if his opponents deny what he conveys about what is forbidden and permitted, he should tell them that their Lord is possessed of a vast mercy that encompasses all creatures: He does not hasten punishment against those who deny Him, nor does He deprive the doer of good of the reward of his deeds. Yet His might and punishment cannot be averted from the guilty people when their time comes. Most commentators identify the deniers as the Jews, following Mujahid and al-Suddi, who claimed they only forbade what Israel had forbidden himself, while others take them to be the polytheists. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand the mercy as the postponement of punishment in this world, and Ibn Kathir notes that the verse pairs encouragement with warning. Tha'lab reads it as a delay of punishment rather than its abolition, and al-Razi, relying on the particle innama, concludes that only four categories of food are forbidden by revelation. Al-Zamakhshari rejects the idea that God would forgo His threats out of generosity. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed after the polytheists objected to the Prophet's claim to forbid certain things. The commentators agree on warning against being reassured by the breadth of divine mercy.

God announces that the polytheists will argue: 'Had God willed, we would not have associated partners with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything.' They take their practices to be willed and approved by God. The commentators agree that this argument is rejected. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi explain that earlier peoples used the same reasoning to deny their prophets until punishment seized them, and that if the argument were sound God would not have punished them. Al-Tabari adds that God refutes their claim that He approved their shirk, and reads the doubled form of the verb as a denial of the messengers. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the denial is total, since whoever ties evil to divine will denies the books and messengers. Ibn 'Atiyya thinks the refutation is implied rather than stated. Al-Razi argues that the verse answers both the Mu'tazilites and the determinists, and distinguishes between will and command. Ibn Sa'di and al-Shinqiti note the difference between universal will, which does not imply approval, and legal will, which does. God then tells His Prophet to ask them: 'Do you have any knowledge that you can bring forth to us?' They have none, and they follow only conjecture and fabrication. Several commentators read the question as mockery and as a challenge. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the reading with the verb in the third person is irregular. All agree that following conjecture in matters of belief is condemned.

God commands His Prophet to tell the idolaters that the conclusive, complete proof belongs to God alone, and that had He willed, He would have guided everyone. Commentators read this as showing that the proof stands against them, not in their favour. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn agree that the 'far-reaching proof' is the complete demonstration that removes every excuse from the one who claims it, present in the Book, the Messenger and clear exposition, and that God, had He willed, would have guided all people. They differ on the meaning of divine will in this verse. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see a will that did not choose to guide the disbeliever and that made people differ. Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites separate this will from the will the pagans invoked to justify their shirk, and hold that God's will cannot be offered as an excuse for unbelief. Al-Razi treats the question at length and answers the Mu'tazilites that guidance by compulsion does not ground obligation. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi explain guidance as the granting of success, distinct from the order of the world. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the variety of paths and proofs belongs to divine wisdom. The commentators present these positions without deciding between them.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to challenge the idolaters who claimed God had forbidden what they themselves had forbidden: bring your witnesses who testify that God prohibited this. The commentators see this as a challenge meant to expose their inability, since they have no genuine witnesses. Al-Tabari, al-Sudi and Mujahid connect the verse to the baheera and sawaiba, while Muqatil applies it to crops and livestock. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi add that the witnesses sought are known for defending this doctrine, and that the aim is to expose them.

If they do bring witnesses, the Prophet must not testify with them, meaning he must not endorse or accept their false testimony, since agreeing would make him one of them, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take this as proof that such witnesses are lying, and Ibn Sa'di holds that an honest person would never testify to such a claim.

Commentators also discuss the word halumma. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that Hijazi speakers keep it unchanged for any number and gender, while Tamimi speakers inflect it. On the phrase 'those who do not believe in the Hereafter', most commentators, including Abu Hayyan, read it as a further description of the same people, whereas al-Naqqash links it to materialists. Abu Hayyan also notes that 'those who denied Our signs' may include the People of the Book. All agree that 'they equate others with their Lord' means giving God equals, such as idols.

This verse tells the Prophet to call people to hear what their Lord truly forbade, not what they invented on conjecture. Commentators agree that the prohibitions form a core set: associating anything with God, failing to honour one's parents, killing children out of fear of poverty, approaching gross sins whether open or hidden, and taking a life without right. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that killing children meant burying infant daughters alive. Most explain imlaq as poverty, though Mu'arrij gives hunger in the Lakhm dialect and Mundhir ibn Sa'id gives spending. On the fawahish, al-Tabari and al-Razi prefer a general meaning covering all sins, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi take the open sin to be street prostitution and the hidden one to be secret liaisons, and Mujahid links them to marriage with forbidden relatives and adultery. The lawful killing is explained as retaliation, stoning of a married adulterer, and apostasy, as in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud quoted by several scholars. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan argue that the commands are implicitly prohibitions of their opposites, since forbidding something entails ordering its contrary. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di make a similar point. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn 'Abbas that these verses are the foundational muhkamat on which all revealed laws agree, and Ka'b al-Ahbar links them to the opening of the Torah. Al-Sha'rawi reads the word ta'alaw as a call to rise above human legislation.

This verse forbids approaching the property of an orphan except in the best way for it, meaning preserving and developing it, and commands giving full measure and weight with justice. It states that God charges no soul beyond its capacity, that one must speak justly even against a relative, and that the covenant made with God must be kept. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that the best way means guarding and growing the wealth, al-Tabari also reporting from Mujahid that it means trading with it, and Ibn Zayd adding that the guardian may eat in reasonable measure if he is poor.

The commentators differ on the meaning of reaching maturity. Al-Sha'bi, Malik and Rabi'a take it as puberty, some adding sound judgement, al-Sudi sets it at thirty years, al-Kalbi between eighteen and thirty, and Abu al-'Aliya as understanding and full strength. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi favour requiring both puberty and good judgement. Al-Tabari notes an implied clause: once maturity and sound judgement are established, the property must be handed back.

On justice in speech, the scholars agree it covers testimony and judgement, and requires truthfulness even toward kin. Regarding the covenant of God, al-Tabari understands it as obedience to God's commands, while al-Mawardi offers two readings: a vow a person has imposed on himself, or an oath sworn by God.

This verse states that the straight path, meaning the religion of Islam and the law of God that He chose for His servants, is one upright way with no crookedness, so believers are commanded to follow it and warned against the other paths such as Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, idol worship and all other creeds and innovations, since following them scatters a person from God's way. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the 'paths' mean innovations, doubts and misguidance, while Ibn Zayd identifies the path as Islam and the other paths as whatever lies outside it. The commentators agree that this command gathers up the orders and prohibitions of the two preceding verses, and that it is an ancient charge carried by all revealed laws; Ibn Abbas considered these verses decisive and not abrogated. Ibn Mas'ud, who transmitted the hadith of the straight line drawn by the Prophet with side lines each guarded by a devil, saw in the straight path what the Prophet had explained. On grammar, the readings differ over 'anna' and 'inna': Ibn Amir, Nafi', 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read 'anna', while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'inna', and al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i connect the phrase to what precedes it. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are correct in meaning. All agree that following this path leads to piety, which is the stated purpose of the command.

This verse states that God gave Moses the Book, meaning the Torah, as a complete favour and an exposition of everything needed in religion, along with guidance and mercy, so that the Children of Israel might believe in meeting their Lord. The commentators agree that the Book is the Torah and that its purpose was to guide the Children of Israel, to set out the laws of their faith, and to lead them to believe in the resurrection and reward. They differ, however, on the meaning of "perfectly, upon the one who did good". Mujahid and Abu 'Ubayda, followed by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi, take it to mean upon the good-doers, that is, a completion of favour toward the righteous among his people, supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading "upon those who did good". Al-Rabi', Qatada and al-Farra' take it to refer to Moses himself, for his good conduct in obedience and in conveying the message. Ibn Zayd understood it as the completion of God's favour toward His prophets. Al-Hasan said that among the people there were both good-doers and wrongdoers, so the Book was sent down as a completion for the good-doers. On "a detailed explanation of all things", Qatada explained it as the lawful and the unlawful, while others took it as the laws and rulings needed. Some commentators read the word "then" as introducing the order of the account rather than the order of time, while others saw it as indicating a difference in rank. These disagreements concern grammar and emphasis rather than the overall meaning of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Qur'an as a Book sent down by God, blessed, meaning abundant in good, benefit and lasting worth. It commands believers to follow it by acting on what it contains, and to be mindful of God, meaning to guard against violating it, in the hope of receiving mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi agree that this Book is the Qur'an, that blessing means an increase of good and benefit in this world and the next, and that following it means acting by its teachings. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse comes after the mention of the Torah to show the Qur'an's superiority as a more complete and more blessed Book. The particle fa in 'follow it' indicates that the Book's greatness makes following it necessary. On the clause introduced by 'an taqulu, the Basrans read it as 'out of fear that you would say', while the Kufans, including al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, read it as 'lest you should say'. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that the aim is to remove any argument from Quraysh and the Arabs that scriptures were sent only to other peoples. On the phrase 'so that you may receive mercy', al-Razi offers several readings of the fear of God, as a means to mercy, a cause of it, or a reward for it. The other commentators cited repeat these meanings without ranking one above another.

The commentators explain that God sent down the blessed Qur'an to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ so that the pagan Arabs could not say on the Day of Judgment that the Book had only been sent down to two groups before them, the Jews and the Christians, and that they had been unaware of their study because it was not in their language. God thus cuts off this argument by revealing the Qur'an in their own tongue. Most agree that the two groups are the Jews and the Christians, that dirasa means reading and recitation, and that the address is to the Quraysh and the Arabs at large. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi hold that the verse establishes the proof and removes any excuse. Ibn 'Atiyya considers it most sound that "an" governs a purpose clause dependent on the sending down, meaning "lest you say" or "out of dislike that you say", whereas the Kufans, including al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, supply "lest" or link it to the command to be mindful of God, while the Basrans supply "out of dislike". Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that "in" here is the light form of "inna" with the lam distinguishing it, and they dispute the Kufan reading on this point. As to ghafla, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as not understanding their language or content. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that these general precepts are common to all nations. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the causal sense here is motive rather than final purpose. The passage continues by stating that the Qur'an brings proof, guidance and mercy, so no one is more unjust than one who denies it and turns away from it, and whose punishment will be severe.

This verse is meant to close off the argument of the idolaters of Quraysh, who might say that the Book was sent only to two earlier communities, the Jews and the Christians, whose study they did not know, or that they would have been better guided had a Book been sent to them. The Qur'an answers that a clear proof has come to them from their Lord, along with guidance and mercy. The commentators agree that the two communities are the Jews and the Christians, and that the verse addresses the pagan Arabs, to whom the Qur'an came in their own tongue. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi take the proof to be the Qur'an itself, while Ibn Kathir notes that it sets out what is lawful and unlawful. Al-Razi observes that it is a proof in what is known by revelation, and guidance in what is known by revelation and reason together. The verse concludes that no one is more unjust than one who denies God's signs and turns away from them. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada read sadafa as turning away, whereas al-Suddi reads it as turning others away, a view Ibn Kathir finds the stronger. Ibn Ashur explains that the evil punishment means its most severe form. The commentators draw few legal conclusions here and focus mainly on linguistic and doctrinal points.

God says that those who turn away from the signs await nothing but the coming of the angels to take their souls, or the coming of your Lord's command, meaning punishment or the judgment on the Day of Resurrection, or the coming of some of the signs of your Lord, which the commentators identify as the signs of the Hour. Most of them, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, take this to mean the sun rising from the west, relying on the authentic hadiths of Abu Hurayra and Abu Dhar. They agree that once that sign appears, faith no longer benefits someone who had not believed before, nor someone who believed but had done no good in his faith, because faith then becomes compelled rather than chosen, and the door of repentance closes. Some say the angels are the angels of death, and that the coming of the Lord means His command of punishment or His judgment on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat these expressions as figurative when applied to God. As for the identity of the sign, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and Qatada hold it is the sun rising from the west, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal mentions the Dajjal, Gog and Magog and the beast of the earth. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi distinguish between a general denial of benefit and a denial limited to that moment, and Ibn 'Atiyya reads the verse in a broader sense. The passage ends with the command to the Prophet to say: wait, we too are waiting, a warning of what is to come.

The verse states that those who split their religion and became rival sects have no connection with the Prophet ﷺ, and that their affair rests with God, who will inform them of what they did on the Day of Judgment. The commentators differ on who is meant. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, and Ibn Abbas in one report, take it to refer to the Jews and Christians, who disagreed about the religion of Abraham, as Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note. Al-Hasan takes it to mean all polytheists, while Abu Hurayra, Umm Salama and Abu Umama take it to mean the people of innovation and desire within this community. Al-Tabari accepts the general sense of division, while judging some reports attributed to the Prophet to be weak. On recitation, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ali read "faraqu" with an alif, meaning they abandoned their religion, while the others read "farraqu" with a doubled letter, meaning they turned the religion into separate doctrines; al-Tabari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan consider the two readings to converge in meaning. The word "shiya'" means factions each following a leader, according to al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. As for "you have no part in them whatsoever," Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read it as a disavowal, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand it as the Prophet not being responsible for their punishment or questioning. Some, including al-Suddi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nahhas, hold that it was abrogated by the verse of fighting; Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir reject this since the verse is a statement that cannot be abrogated, and al-Tabari finds no contradiction with the command to fight.

This verse states that God repays whoever brings a good deed with ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed only with its equal, so that no one is wronged. Commentators differ on what the terms mean. Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and Abu Salih, followed by al-Tabari in several reports, take the good deed to be the declaration 'There is no god but God' and the evil deed to be association with God (shirk). Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold that the verse is general and covers every good and bad deed; al-Razi argues that a ruling tied to a fitting attribute extends with that attribute. Ibn 'Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri report that it was revealed about the Bedouins, while the emigrants receive seven hundred fold for a good deed; Ibn 'Atiyya says this report needs a firm chain. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi take ten to be the minimum multiplication promised, and the number to signify abundance rather than a fixed limit, since the promise reaches seven hundred and beyond; Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan lean toward reading the number literally. Ibn Kathir cites many hadiths on the multiplication of good deeds. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and others explain that the equal recompense for evil reflects divine justice, while the multiplication of good reflects grace. The reading of al-Hasan and Ya'qub, 'ashrun amthaluha' with nominative endings, is accepted as grammatically sound. All agree on the closing phrase: God neither reduces the reward of the doer of good nor adds to the punishment of the wrongdoer.

This verse reports that the Prophet ﷺ declares that his Lord has guided him to a straight path, an upright and firm religion, the creed of Abraham the hanif, who was not among the polytheists. The commentators explain that "dinan" is either an apposition replacing "sirat" or the object of an implied verb such as "He made me know". Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take "qiyaman" to mean upright and steadfast, and hold that the two readings, qayyiman and qiyaman, have the same meaning, though al-Tabari prefers the emphatic form as the more eloquent. As for "hanifan", most understand it as one who turns away from falsehood toward truth, while Ibn Qutayba links it to uprightness.

The exegetes agree that the verse comes after the condemnation of the polytheists and of those who split their religion, affirming that guidance comes from God alone and that Abraham was a monotheist. Ibn Kathir stresses that all the prophets called to Islam in the sense of worshipping God alone, and that the Prophet ﷺ, though commanded to follow Abraham's way, perfected it. Ibn 'Ashur sees Islam as carrying forward the principles of Abraham: monotheism, harmony with human nature, and gratitude.

The following verses declare that prayer, sacrifice, life and death belong to God, Lord of the worlds. Commentators differ on "nusuki": Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada take it as the sacrifice of the pilgrimage, al-Hasan as religion, and az-Zajjaj as worship. Al-Qurtubi and others report these views without choosing among them, treating them as complementary.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to declare that his prayer, his sacrifice, his life and his death belong entirely to Allah, Lord of the worlds, with no partner, unlike the idols the polytheists worship. The commentators agree on the core meaning: total sincerity toward God in worship, in life and in death. Most understand nusuk as the ritual sacrifice, especially the sacrifice of the Hajj and 'Umrah, as Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Qatada say; Ibn Kathir notes that prayer and sacrifice are joined in the verse 'pray to your Lord and sacrifice.' Al-Hasan takes it to mean religion, al-Zajjaj means worship in general, and al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy extend it to all acts of obedience.

On life and death, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that God alone controls them, or that life is devoted to obedience and death to the return to His reward. Al-Mawardi adds a third sense: one's deeds in life and one's final bequests. Ibn 'Ashur suggests death may also refer to the spiritual states of the Prophet after his death. Al-Razi notes that sincerity is a condition for the validity of prayer, a legal point he presents without deciding it.

As for 'I am the first of the Muslims', Qatada and al-Hasan take it to mean the first of this community, while others read it as the first of all, since the Prophet precedes the other prophets in creation. Ibn Kathir prefers the first reading. Finally, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya mention variant readings of mahyaya, including Nafi's pronunciation with a sukun on the yā', and of nusuki.

God instructs His Prophet to answer those who invited him to worship their idols with a rhetorical rebuke: should I seek a lord other than God, who is the Lord of everything? Every other being is a creature under His dominion, so no one can share in His lordship. The commentators agree that « no soul earns except against itself » means that each person bears only the consequences of his own deeds, good or bad, and that « no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another » means that no sinner carries another's sin. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed in response to Quraysh, who offered the Prophet to return to their religion and take on any consequences himself. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi state that the address concerns the polytheists, from whom the Prophet disassociates himself. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that wizr originally means a heavy load and then came to mean sin. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the verse as a reply to their call to carry the sins of others. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir hold that the return to God on the Day of Resurrection will settle what people disputed, including matters concerning the Prophet himself. On « He made you successors on the earth », al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand successive generations replacing one another, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers the community of Muhammad to be the last of the nations. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see the differences in rank and provision as a test from God. Al-Qurtubi notes that some jurists, including al-Shafi'i, derived from this verse the invalidity of selling another's property without authority, while Abu Hanifa and others, relying on the report of Urwa al-Bariqi, accept such a sale subject to the owner's approval.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls Allah's favour in making humans successors on the earth, one generation following another, and in raising some of them above others in degrees of provision, strength, wealth, rank and knowledge. All of this is a trial meant to reveal who is grateful. They differ on the meaning of succession. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, took it to mean that humans replaced the jinn who once inhabited the earth; Ibn Qutayba understood it as people succeeding one another; al-Zajjaj and others held that the community of Muhammad succeeded all earlier nations, since he is the seal of the prophets. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi also mention that humans are Allah's vicegerents who manage the earth, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi list the same possibilities without preferring one. The commentators agree that the degrees refer to differences in provision, strength and dignity, and that the trial is a test. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di add differences in character, talent, health and sickness. As for the statement that your Lord is swift in punishment, most explain that whatever is to come is near, so the punishment of the Hereafter is near too; others understand worldly punishment for those who deserve it, and Ibn Bahr links its swiftness to Allah's will. The verse goes on to say He is Forgiving and Merciful, joining warning and hope. Al-Sa'di and others note that these attributes encourage obedience and warn against disobedience.
